utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How long a prison sentence did you serve in Gradisce?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there together with Petar Sale and another person in the same cell; right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same penitentiary, but we were not in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you know, later, that the state security service recorded your activities with the third person that you were with?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct -- I mean, I imagine that you do know that at that time you were monitored, taken care of, I don't know how to put it, by Milanko Orescanin, an operations officer of the state security service?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He worked at the state security service in Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear that name, and in Slavonski Brod, I was there only a few times in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had very detailed information about your activities concerning that person. Tell me: Do you know anything about that? Because there is evidence that after the HDZ victory, you were the person who gave instructions to have that operations officer killed, the man from Slavonski Brod, and he was liquidated on the 15th of August, 1991, a religious holiday, Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first I ever hear of it. I never held any executive positions and I had no influence whatsoever on anyone's liberty or life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there are persons, there are witnesses, Mr. Mesic, who according to your instructions kidnapped that person, Mijokovic, Milan from Slavonski Brod and Jokic, Ivan from Slavonski Brod?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably the one who is socialising with them. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also according to your instructions, Momo Devrnja, a Serb from Orahovac, a forwarder was liquidated, a man who had a conflict with you. I imagine you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as much influence as I had on Lincoln's assassination. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of December, Muselinovic, Miodrag with his wife Milici and neighbour Desanka Radonjic [phoen] was the chief of SUP in Orahovac and he was killed according to your instructions.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same answer as for the previous one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question. The speed is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to pause. The interpreters can't keep up this pace. Now, you both speak the same language; therefore, it would be better if there was a pause between the question and answer. And also after the answer. Mr. Milosevic, will you bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to your instructions, Serb villages Pusina, Kokocak, Kraskovici [phoen], Brekoracani [phoen], Gornja Pistana, Slatinski Drenovac were destroyed; is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with actual facts. I found out about the torching of these villages and I protested. I launched by protest with President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With who?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With President Tudjman, and you had also socialised with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in the Hefner affair in 1967, the one that had to do with the selling of white slaves, and also you remember that Tito referred to an affair that you were involved in that had to do with buying machinery for the textile industry in Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is just a figment of someone's imagination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were the main organiser of the affair that had to do with military records, abolishing the security records that were kept? Need I remind you of why you did that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is no affair. This has to do with the following: The National Defence authorities kept records about young men who were supposed to go and do their military service. As president of the municipality, I got information that Croats were not being sufficiently active in the army, that they did not enroll in military schools. They did not take up commissions and they did not go to military schools in general. I was surprised by the fact that it was only Serbs who were applying. I realised that there was one particular item in questionnaires, that is to say, item 32, and this was something that was filled by the officials of the Secretariats of National Defence and I asked to see what was written there. Since a person involved protested because it said that his father -- his name is Slavko Sulovnjak. He was in the army. And in that questionnaire, it said that his father was an Ustasha from 1941 and that he was tried as a war criminal. However, his father had been a partisan. His father had retired as an non-commissioned officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. I asked for this to be looked into. They did look into it and they established that for over 90 per cent of Croatian young men, it said that they were children of enemies, and that therefore they could not attend such schools. Serb children did have passing grades, though, so to speak. That is what I know about item 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what the Croatian authorities wrote. It was not the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Serbs who were employed in the National Defence authorities, and I can even give you names if you're really interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that Croats were not employed in Croatia in National Defence authorities?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is only when I came to Orahovac as president of the municipality, the first Croat became head of the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that while you were in prison, and this Petar Sale, by the way, is a well-known chauvinist from Sibenik; is that right? While you were in prison, the officials of the state security service of Croatia tried to employ your services for the rest of your prison term?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this is a figment of your imagination. I did have a prison sentence of two years and two months. This was the first-instance court that made that ruling. However, the Supreme Court reduced the sentence to one year and I served one year. I don't really see why anybody would try to enlist my services. This is again pure fantasy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, remind us again: When was this prison sentence? What years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From 1975, from May 1975 until May 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after that you worked for the state security service of Croatia in the sector for internal enemies at that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. The next question is: What was the sentence imposed for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For participation in the Croatian Spring. I was president of a municipality and I took part in the Croatian Spring, as it was called. I can also give you a list of all the crimes that I was accused of, if the Trial Chamber is interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was this Croatian Spring?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the crimes was that I said: Let the devil get warm by our Croatian fire but let him not extinguish the fire. At that time, a topical question throughout Yugoslavia was the struggle for constitutional amendments. I said for all of those who wish to see democracy, there is place in the train leading to democracy. Every person who tries to sidetrack that train by putting his foot in front of it can only remain without that foot. That's what I said. I also said that the Croats tread their path to the Adriatic Sea with their own sabres and all the rest followed in their footsteps. These are the crimes for which I was sentenced to two years, two months in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you worked then for the state security service of Croatia in the department for internal enemies and that after that you started working for the state security service of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth is that I asked for a passport. For 15 years I did not have a passport. I asked for a passport to be issued to me as a free citizen. I was refused a passport, and I lodged a complaint because of that. And I did that every year, a few times every year, as a matter of fact. That is more or less all the contact I had with the police. All the rest just pertains to the realm of fantasy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You did not work for the state security service of Croatia, you did not work for the counter-intelligence service of the army, I assume. And it is assumed that your relationship with Spegelj dates back to those days, that is to say, some other period of time. Do you know that Franjo Tudjman replaced Spegelj as well because it was his suspicion that he was an agent of the KOS and that is why he fled across the border with the assistance of Josip Manolic, former head of the Croatian police, with a false passport issued in a false name?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is pure fantasy and that can be proved by the following: In order to get a job after prison, I applied at 150 different posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish. Yes. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was different, and it had to do with Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish and give his explanation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the logic? Why would I work for the state security service and I could not find a job? And I applied at 150 different places, and I did not get a job anywhere. What is the logic of that? And for 15 years I did not have a passport. As for Spegelj, the situation was well known. At a meeting of the Croatian political leadership, Spegelj presented a plan, which is referred to in Croatia as the Spegelj Plan. He proposed that warehouses be seized from the Yugoslav People's Army, where weapons were, depots with the weapons of the Yugoslav People's Army, and not to touch military barracks but to take weapons. Since in these depots there were several hundreds or perhaps thousands of tanks, Spegelj said: If we take these weapons, for each tank we have people who are trained, who were in the army, and if Milosevic wants to move against Croatia, we have the resources to meet him. In this way, we are going to avoid a war, because the Yugoslav army is in disarray. However, if we go on waiting, the Yugoslav army will consolidate itself, it's going to become a Serb army, and Milosevic is going for try to conquer Croatian territories with it. Tudjman disagreed with that. I was the only one who voted in favour of that proposal, and that is why General Spegelj left his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you really have this hang-up about Milosevic. You mentioned me in every other sentence you uttered yesterday. On the basis of what you said just now, Mr. Mesic, is that to show that you were more radical than Tudjman in your viewpoints that had to do with the war, more radical than Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really pleased that this question was put to me, because I responded in one case how war can be averted; to take weapons from the hands of the army and to avoid the war. Because Croatia would have something to meet Milosevic with if he were to attack. So this is a case about which I think I was right until the present day, and I think that General Spegelj was right too. Many lives would have been saved, both of Serbs and Croats, had it been that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, is it clear to you, in connection with these accusations levelled against Milosevic, and Milosevic's purported command over the army, what you said just now, that I really had -- had I actually had the possibility of commanding the army, Yugoslavia would not have fallen apart, there would not have been a civil war. Regrettably, I did not have that possibility, so what happened, happened. But please answer the following: You spoke about motives a few minutes ago. Motive for a cooperation with the state security service. Could your motive not have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been to reduce your prison sentence from two years to one year? You said it yourself. Just like now, the motive for cooperation here is to avoid punishment and responsibility that is your due, since you are a person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know you have to ask questions here and not make speeches. The witness has said that he did not cooperate with the state security service, so there seems little point going on about it. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the subject, that we're discussing such questions: On the 24th of April -- on the 26th of April, 1994, you stated for Feral Tribune: There were quite a few murders in the case of which the perpetrators, though known, are not in prison yet. People know who killed Reihl-Kir and Saban Krivokuca, the Zec family. The murders of the Zec family said themselves that they raped the woman and her 12-year-old daughter and killed them. One of them is employed by the Ministry of Defence. You know it's not easy to sit at the same table with a person whose bodyguard took a 12-year-old child, followed a bullet into his head and then threw him into the garbage. It is my understanding that it has become clear to the Croat people as well that things have happened that are leading us to an abyss. So that is your own statement, isn't it? I have quoted you correctly, I believe. My question is: The changes in Croatia - you are now president of Croatia - is this fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us first of all deal with the quotation which you have attributed to the witness. Mr. Mesic, that is a quotation from a paper in April 1994. Is the quotation correct, and is there anything you want to say about it before we move on to another subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I always struggled for the rule of law, and I did assert that crimes had been committed, and the rule of law had to prevail. I am struggling for the rule of law now as well. I'm struggling for ascertaining individual guilt and responsibility, because in that case, collective responsibility will be halted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. My question was: The changes in Croatia which have taken place, and you have been elected president, has that led to this clearing up and settling of accounts with the killers that you yourself said were known, that their names were known, the people who did the killings were known? Now, you, as head of the Croatian state now, have you succeeded in clearing all this up and bringing these people to justice?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that you are talking about in this particular case are undergoing trial in Croatia at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean all the victims that you mentioned, or just some of them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones that we learnt about have been taken to trial, but none of the cases have been completed, no files have been closed, and investigations are under way and the perpetrators will be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you yourself feel responsible for what took place and for the crimes that were committed while you yourself occupied the highest posts and offices in Croatia after Tudjman, that is to say, up until 1994?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused knows very well, because he's a lawyer, that I was president of the Croatian Sabor or parliament assembly, which means primus inter pares, and I was president of parliament. I was not in the judiciary organs or in executive power and authority, nor was I in the police force. And the accused knows full well what the function of a parliament is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, you were president of the executive board of the HDZ party as well.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the president of the executive board of the HDZ. That's true, in 1992, which means from January to the elections, that is to say, until October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you were prime minister when the HDZ won the elections; isn't that right, Mr. Mesic, when it came into power?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. You have the right facts and figures. I was prime minister for three months. That is true. And after that I took up my post as member of the Yugoslav state Presidency. And that's where I remained until the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What you're saying is that after you returned from the Yugoslav state Presidency, when you were elected as president of the Croatian parliament, that that was not the second most important office in Croatia and that you link your activities up with the formal decisions taken by -- official decisions taken by parliament and not for the overall political situation in Croatia, the state of affairs that prevailed and everything that went on there. You were the number two man in Croatia; isn't that right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always strove for the functioning of the rule of law of the Croatian state and the Croatian constitution recognises the division of power into three sections: The legal section and the two others, the judiciary and everything else that the constitution implied and stipulated, which means that I was president of parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You therefore consider that you worked in line with the constitution and that you did the work that comes under the competencies of the parliament. Does the parliament have the right to send Croatian troops, for example, to Bosnia-Herzegovina or is that something that comes under the competence of executive power?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very good thing that this question was raised, and I think we ought to clear it up now. For the Croatian army to be able to act outside Croatia, the head of state could take a decision only with the acquiescence and agreement from the Croatian parliament. This kind of agreement was never issued by the Croatian parliament, whether anybody went outside Croatia, groups or individuals, it was not up to the parliament to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. What you're saying is that you don't consider yourself to be responsible for not having carried out your constitutional duties, the ones that you insisted upon a moment ago, because parliament did not take decisions in that respect, the decisions that it should have taken. So you feel, do you, that this rids you of all responsibility?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that, for example, units of the Republic of Croatia launched an attack on the municipality of Brod in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 26th of March, 1992, a great crime was committed there, the population of the village of Sijekovac in the Bosanski Brod municipality was massacred and even at that time Bosnia-Herzegovina was not even internationally recognised, which means that in all respects it was part and parcel of Yugoslavia, even in the most -- in the strictest formal sense. And their 108 -- the members of the 108th Brigade of the National Guard Corps were there from Slavonski Brod and so on and so forth. There is a complete set of documents pertaining to the perpetrators. Is it possible that you, as president of parliament, did not know about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several interventions that I had from several families of -- and the parents said that they had gone to Bosnia. I asked for information, both from the head of state and the defence minister, and they told me that it was only volunteers who had gone and that it was the volunteers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina who volunteered to go. I had no other instruments at my disposal. The only thing I could do was to ask to be informed. But I must say that if anybody does have knowledge as to the fact that a citizen of Croatia perpetrated a crime anywhere, then this should be filed. Croatia is a country in which the rule of law holds true today, and everybody will be held accountable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've received many such reports, Mr. Mesic, but are you saying now that you did not know, as president of parliament, a body who was the sole body competent to take a decision in the matter, that you did not know that what came within the frameworks of your competence was done illegally and that you did not in fact know that Croatian troops were present in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That observation is quite correct. I did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you know, for example, that from the 3rd of April until the 9th of April an attack was launched on Kupres, the Gornji Malovan, Kratez, Mala Plazenica, Zagliska Suma [phoen], the town of Kupres, Begovo Selo, all these other villages, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is looks as though this is going to be a reputation of much of the cross-examination which we heard in the earlier part of the case, which doesn't relate to the evidence of the witness. What he said is that he heard of interventions, made inquiries and was told that it was due to volunteers. Perhaps, Mr. Mesic, in order to avoid a long list being given, if that's what the accused has in mind, can you answer this question: Can you tell us where these interventions which you inquired about took place, or can you not now remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly do not know the locations they were sent to, but the parents of the young men told us that their children had gone to Bosnia. When I asked about this, the defence minister and the former president of the Republic told me that not a single unit had gone, that it was only volunteers who had gone, and that is the volunteers who were actually born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I had no other instruments for investigating the truthfulness of those assertions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, it wasn't a case of individuals, for example, if we had the 106th Brigade from Osijek, the full complement of it, and the Zuti Mravi from Vukovar, the 101 Zagreb Brigade, the Student King Tomislav Battalion, the Zrinjski Battalion, the special purpose unit of the MUP of Croatia and so on and so forth. In addition to the KOS, the Zenga, and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause there, Mr. Milosevic. The witness can only give evidence about what he knew himself. Now, what is being suggested, that these units intervened in your inquiries, were those units mentioned? Do you know anything about them or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that the accused knows the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina very well and that he is well aware of all the units that went to war there, and I'm sure he could enumerate all the Serbs units. If he knows about the Croatian units, I'm sure he knows much more about those who came from Belgrade and other towns and destroyed Croatian and Bosnian towns. However, let me respond once again and say that I did not know of a single unit which went from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. Is it true that your nephew, who was not a volunteer and who is not from Bosnia-Herzegovina, also went to Bosnia-Herzegovina with his unit? Do you know about that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My nephews were not in the army. They were too young to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that later on. But tell me this: How can you, for example, as we spoke a moment Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ago about those incidents and what was going on, to all intents and purposes an aggression, and you say you know nothing about it, this is what I have in my hand: The command for the rear of Bosanski Brod Sijekovac. That is where the crimes were perpetrated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you now. The witness has given his evidence. He knows nothing about it. Your duty, your function at the moment, is to cross-examine him about his evidence. It's not to make speeches or try and present evidence yourself. Now, he's given his evidence about this matter and he can take it no further. In due course, if it's relevant, you can call evidence, but for the moment you must move on to some other topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I wish to ask the witness respect to what he says he didn't know, how he can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's told you. He told you he doesn't know. He doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His comment on this military document and this is something that will take me 20 seconds to read out. This is a photocopy with a stamp and signature. It is a permit allowing the intervention platoon from Zagreb, a certificate, in fact, to execute the detention of women --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it signed by the witness? What connection does it have with him, before you put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The connection it has is -- with the witness is -- this is to say, it is linked with his second function in the hierarchy of the Republic of Croatia, and this is a certificate issued to the intervention platoon from Zagreb, which is the capital of Croatia, where the cabinet of Mr. Mesic is located, a permit allowing the detention of women, young girls, Serbs, for the needs of the male sex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the connection with this witness, before you put it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the connection is to show that the units that he says he knows nothing about are not only committing crimes but are organising rape and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, that's nothing to do with the witness. You're here to cross-examine him about these matters. If it's relevant, you can call evidence in due course, but what you're not here to do is to make speeches and try and present evidence that crimes were committed by the other side which are irrelevant. Now, this trial, remember, this indictment, is about crimes which are alleged -- it's alleged that you committed, and his evidence is about that, so you should concentrate on that rather than to try and show that crimes were committed by others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just raise a few matters, because it's plainly important to the accused. Perhaps what is at stake here is the credibility of this particular witness for the Prosecution. In respect of this, the accused is attempting, I believe, to put forward to the Court various events that occurred during his Presidency of Croatia, to demonstrate his involvement within the conflict that occurred in the region. Those issues may well be important to this accused in relation to issues of defence of territory, other aspects of the conflict. I don't have instructions on that matter, so I can't say, but it may well be that it's the form of questioning that's the problem here. But it's the issue of what was happening at the time whilst he was president of Croatia and whilst troops were leaving the borders of his state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, much time has been wasted in this trial in trying to establish that crimes were committed by others, which may or may not be relevant to the trial. That is why it's important to see whether documents were signed by this witness. If the issue is that it was notorious, if that's the point that is being made, that crimes were being put, were being made, were being committed, then that can be put to the witness. What can't be put, which is what I suspect the accused is doing, is to read out lists and lists of crimes, taking up time, and thereby, in my view, raising matters which at this stage are not relevant to the trial. Our time is limited. We must stick to the relevant matters. But I will put to the witness the general point, and we'll hear what he says. Mr. Mesic, what may be being suggested is this, and you can help us, if you would: That it was well known that crimes were being committed in Bosnia during the time of your Presidency. I think this is what is being suggested. And therefore you must have known about these matters, apart from them being referred to by the parents of the volunteers or members of the armed forces, as you suggested. Now, if that is being suggested, then you should answer it. Was this a matter which in fact was something of general knowledge in Croatia, and in particular, to you as president at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was the president of the parliament, I knew about the camps organised by the Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I received information, and this was actually shown on television ultimately. If there were other crimes, news of them did not reach me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until when were you president of parliament, Mr. Mesic? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was president of parliament from the 7th of September, 1992 until the 24th of May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 1994. Very well. In that period of time, I ask you, within that period of time, what you said you don't know, and you said you inquired of the minister about -- let me tell you: On the 3rd of July, 1993, Alois Mok criticised the Croats because of their activities against the Muslims, and he issued a protest which he addressed to the government of Croatia. On the 4th of February, also while you were president of parliament, the Security Council of the United Nations -- let me repeat- the Security Council of the United Nations, neither more nor less, issued a statement warning Croatia that it would be exposed to serious consequences if it did not withdraw its regular troops from Bosnia within a period of two months. So this is issued by the Security Council. It was a presidential statement. And yet you, as the president of parliament, say you did not know about this. On the same day, the German chancellor, Helmut Kohl?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with the Security Council point and then you can tell us what is the relevance of this, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's really noteworthy that the accused is now expressing remorse for the sufferings of the Bosniak people. This is really something to be commended. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you deal with the Security Council resolution, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect the resolution, I have already said what I was able to do was to ask the president of the state whether our troops had crossed the border. He said no. The Minister of Defence said no. I had no other instruments at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. May we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not going to proceed with this until you've explained what the relevance is. The indictment charges you with crimes in Croatia in the period between 1990 and 1992. What relevance does the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats have in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what we are speaking of here is not relevance, but rather, the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. You can ask questions about the credibility -- wait a moment. You can ask questions relating to the credibility of the witness, but of course you're bound by his answers and the questions can only go so far as to test their credibility. Now, he's given you an answer about the Security Council resolution. Your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. Then I may proceed to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You arrived on the 5th of December in the Croatian parliament. You thanked them for their confidence. This was on the 5th of December, 1991. And you made a notorious statement to the effect that you thought I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more. Is this so, Mr. Mesic? We saw it on the video we played here a few days ago, and all of Yugoslavia knows about this. You said: I think I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An excellent question. I will explain what this was about. The Croatian parliament elected me to be the Croatian member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. I went to Belgrade, where first, for several months, I was not allowed to take up my duties because the Federal Assembly was unable to meet. After that, the Serbian bloc boycotted my election as president under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let him finish. You've asked him a question. Let him give his explanation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finally, under pressure from the international community, I was elected president. Croatia adopted a decision on its independence. Croatia, in agreement with the international community, postponed its secession from Yugoslavia by three months. This time period had elapsed. Yugoslavia no longer existed. The federal institutions were no longer functioning. I returned to Zagreb, and that's precisely what I said. Because I did not go to Belgrade to open up a house-painting business. I went there as a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Since Yugoslavia no longer existed and the Presidency no longer existed, I had performed the tasks entrusted to me by the Croatian parliament and was reporting back, ready to take up a different office. What was I to do in Belgrade when the Presidency no longer existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mesic. This is truly worthy of admiration, your explanation of what you said, but you haven't told me whether you actually said: I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused is a lawyer. He understands very well what I'm talking about. My task was to represent Croatia in the Federal Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for you to repeat this. You said this in the Croatian or Serbian language, or whatever you want to call it, and everybody understood it. Your explanation now is obviously an attempt to make this statement relative, but this is no longer important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your public statements, or rather, in Tudjman's public statements on Ban Jelacic Square on the 24th of May, 1992, said "There would have been no war had not Croatia wanted it. But we thought that it was only by war that we could win the independence of Croatia. That's why we had a policy of negotiations behind which we were setting up military units. Had this not been so, we would not have reached our goal." Is this correct, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this could have been reported only by the Serbian press, because it simply does not correspond to the truth. We know who was in control of the press in Serbia. It was the accused, Slobodan Milosevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, a few days ago we watched a video of this, and we saw this speech on Ban Jelacic square, taped on video. Tell me, please: Do you know that when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was founded and the new constituted was promulgated on the 27th of April, 1992, a declaration was adopted on the goals of the new common state, that is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, according to which, and I quote verbatim: "Yugoslavia has no territorial pretensions towards any of the former Yugoslav republics." Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the declaration on the establishing of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia says, but I do know everything that was done to cut off parts of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and annex them to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you're telling us fairy tales about Karlovac, Karlobag Virovitica boundary. When did you ever hear any official of the Republic of Serbia referring to this border, and when did any body or organ of the Republic of Serbia or anyone in Yugoslavia raise this issue and talk about such a boundary? This is a pure fabrication that you are launching here. Where did you get this idea?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite understandable that those who perpetrated aggression did not make such statements, but the Serbian minister, who was in the government, one of the ministers of Mr. Milosevic, visited this boundary with Vojislav Seselj, the Chetnik Vojvoda or leader, to show how far the interests of Serbia reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What minister are you referring to? And if a minister visits a spot, if he goes to a certain municipality, does he go to a boundary or does he mark a boundary? Was he marking a boundary there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understand very well that if someone visits Croatia, especially an official, he should visit the official organs of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What municipal organs are you referring to if someone is visiting a municipality? I didn't know you were a police state of that kind, that someone visiting a municipality in Croatia would have to report to the police.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not paid to teach the accused Croatian laws. I was paid to implement them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you are a university graduate. Did you ever learn about the rights of peoples to self-determination, and do you know that volumes and volumes of books have been written on this topic? Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this question is pointless. Of course I do. Of course I know about the right to self-determination. This is going too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, then answer me, please: Where did you get the idea that, as you said, the Serbs in Croatia do not have a right to self-determination? Where did you get the idea, as you said on page 2 of your statement, that according to the constitution of 1974, Yugoslavia was a confederal state? You know yourself that this is untrue. Show me a single constitutional provision to this effect. Is this correct or not, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Yugoslavia was established as a confederal institution because all decisions were made for the most part by consensus, and the accused knows this very well. He also knows very well that according to the constitution of 1974, the republics were called states, and he also knows that, by virtue of their association into Yugoslavia, they also had the right to disassociate themselves from Yugoslavia. When a threat arose that Croatia and Slovenia might suffer the same fate as Kosovo, Vojvodina, and Montenegro, Croatia made use of its right to disassociate itself, and the Badinter Commission confirmed this. Of course the Serbs have a right to their own state. That state is the Republic of Serbia. But it is well known that national minorities cannot ask to secede from the Republic of Croatia. They could ask for that but they could not realise it, because the Republic of Croatia was recognised in the borders established by Avnoj and the accused knows this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that according to the Yugoslav constitution, it was the peoples and not the republics that had sovereignty? Do you remember that even the coat of arms of Yugoslavia had five torches, represented five peoples: The Serbs, the Croats, the Slovenes, the Macedonians and the Montenegrins, and then later on a sixth torch was added when the Muslims were declared a constituent people? Are you aware of this, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constituent elements of the Federation were the republics, plus two autonomous provinces: Vojvodina, and Kosovo. Those were the constituent elements of the Federation. Symbolism is one thing, but constitutional provisions are quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You assert that in the constitutions of Yugoslavia and the republics, it was not the sovereignty of peoples that was the starting point but the territory of the republics established in 1945; is that what you're claiming? I just want to be clear so as not to waste time.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said what I had to say about the constituent elements of the Federation. Croatia had the right to self-determination, and the Serbs in Croatia had the right to protection, to protection of their collective rights and of their status as citizens of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed, then. Let us proceed at a faster pace, so please answer me yes or no: Is it correct that all the constitutions of Croatia, until the amendments introduced by you in 1990, had a provision about the Serbs as a constituent people, not a ethnic minority, as you have just said? For example, the constitution of 1945, 1963, 1974, the constitutional amendments of July 1990. So these amendments of July 1990 for the first time left out the Serbs as a constituent element of the Republic of Croatia. I'm referring now to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia. Did all the constitutions contain a provision about the Serbian people as a constituent people in Croatia; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot reply to this question with yes or no. The constitutions were enacted in different periods of time, in different situations, and in different international environments. The constitution, therefore, had different provisions at different points in time. For example, the Yugoslav and the Croatian constitutions had a provision which other constitutions, for example, do not contain, that there are two kinds of groups: Narodi and Narodnosti, two kinds of peoples, plus ethnic groups. The constitution was further developed up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the fact that the Serbs were left out of the constitution was a development. Do you know that on the 14th of May, 1887, the Croatian parliament enacted a provision on the use of the Cyrillic alphabet? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that particular piece of information, but I do thank the accused for having given me this piece of information. That is truly meaningful for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the rest, that what the constitution -- what the assembly of Croatia adopted in 1887 was abolished in 1990 by your parliament? They abolished the Cyrillic alphabet as an official alphabet. Do you know about that? You went 150 years backwards. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet another piece of information, very important to me, as a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. Do you remember an entire series of laws, not to mention taking over symbols, the symbols of the Nazi state of the independent state of Croatia, for example, the law on the Academy of Sciences and Arts, the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts? In article 1 it says that it is the legal successor of the academy from the period from 1941 to 1945. The budget for 1991 does not envisage a single dinar for the schools of Serbs in Croatia, but it does envisage money for Italians, Czechs, Ruthenians, and other national minorities. The law on the government allows the government to take measures against so-called disobedient municipalities. The only executive government in Europe that has the right to dissolve municipalities. The law on education refers to the Croatian language only, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. What is the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is -- the question is: Is it correct that not only through this behaviour and also the combination of this ethnic intolerance towards the Serbs, but it is also through the adoption of many laws, the Croatian authorities instigated nationalism and chauvinism not only in Croatia but also a discriminatory, an insulting attitude towards Serbs in Croatia. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia adopted laws that gave equal rights to all its citizens and protect national minorities, all vulnerable groups, actually. National minorities are vulnerable groups, and that is why Croatia favours positive discrimination of all vulnerable groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then give me a comment with regard to these following statements: There are many such laws, and of course they did have to cause concern. For example, a meeting of the parliament on the 4th of October, 1990, the 4th of October, 1990, your own assembly. Damir Majovic says: "Do not trust the Serbs even when they bring gifts." Stjepan Sulimanac says: "Persons who moved in after 1918, who moved into Croatia after 1918, a law should be passed with regard to such persons and there should be protection from them." Then MP Ivan Milas says: "We are going to use a sword in respect of your rights. The day of a final showdown is getting near." Another MP says: "All Serbs should be isolated like Iraq isolated the Kurds. A ghetto should be established for the Serbs." And Praljak, what's his name, one of the helmsmen of the HDZ said in April 1990: "Outside the boys are already singing we are going to slaughter the Serbs." And so on and so forth. Is that the right kind of atmosphere, Mr. Mesic? Is that the atmosphere in which the Serbs were supposed to view everything that was happening to them with confidence? And in the meantime you dismissed practically all Serbs from the state administration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. Now, you've read out a series -- you've read out a series of quotations which are said to have been made in the parliament. Now, Mr. Mesic, you can deal with that. First of all, do you know if these statements were made, or these sort of statements, and if so, is there anything that you can tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were different statements that will were impermissible, and it is certain that such statements harmed Croatia. As for Slobodan Praljak, I must say that he was never a member of the HDZ. When the HDZ was established, he was one of President Tudjman's major critics. Now, why were such statements made? I say today as well that they did not work to Croatia's advantage but to its disadvantage. There were rallies of Serbs in various places on the 4th of February, 1990. On the 4th of March, 1990, there was a rally in Petrova Gora of people from Lika, Kordun, Banja Luka, Bosanska Krajina, and also Vojvodina in Serbia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that when Ante Markovic established his own party?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of July, 1990, the Serb assembly passed its so-called decision on Serb autonomy in Croatia. On the 1st of July, 1990 in Kosovo by Knin, an official statement was made that the Serb Autonomous Krajina was established in Croatia, its president being Milan Babic. On the 17th of August, the first roadblocks were on the road in Benkovac, Knin and Gradacac. On the 13th of September, there were meetings and rallies of persons in Dvor and in various other places. In towns and in municipalities in Croatia where there is a predominantly Serb population, there were inscriptions saying: "This is Serbia." So it is persons who came from Serbia who manipulated the Serb masses in Serbia? Why? Because Milosevic needed to bring about an insurgency of the Serbs in Croatia so that he would light the initial fuse for setting Bosnia-Herzegovina on fire, because he needed Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what the accused actually did. That is why he should be held accountable. These radical statements, regrettably, are only in response to statements made by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you see that you're not testifying about anything here except your political and propaganda activities all this time? Because you do not have a single fact here; you only have your own positions and your attacks against Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the trial of the accused Slobodan Milosevic. I have sufficient facts in order to believe that he is guilty because he planned war, he carried out war, and he built into this plan a crime that he should be held accountable for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us get back to the subject-matter of the trial. Yes. You are asking about the statements, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I put a question. I said: These laws and the atmosphere in parliament, the atmosphere in Croatia, the dismissals of thousands of persons from the administration, from the police, from the media, even from the health sector, is that the kind of atmosphere that caused concern among the Serbs, or was it, as Mr. Mesic just put it now, was it Milosevic who caused concern and who led to this insurgency? Were these facts of life the thing that caused concern among them or did Milosevic come from Serbia to make them start a rebellion, now that I've quoted all of this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the accused Milosevic who came. His emissaries came, and they were the ones who started the insurgency in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you deal with the allegations which are made, that, first of all, there were the dismissals of thousands of persons from the administration and the police and the media and the health sector? Now, can you deal with that, Mr. Mesic? Were thousands dismissed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is an exaggeration to speak of thousands, but that there were dismissals is a fact. There were unnecessary dismissals. People also took those who dismissed them to court and won these cases. I think that these statements that are radical and inadmissible only work to Croatia's detriment, and I always struggled against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the atmosphere and the statements -- I mean, you say now that it is negative, but the atmosphere was there, wasn't it? So it's not Milosevic who caused an insurgency among the Serbs; it is your laws, your pressures, your behaviour, your attacks against people. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to reply once again, and I've already said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you've already said it, please don't read out what you've already read out, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who wanted to cut off parts of Croatia, parts of the Republic of Croatia, those are the ones who are to be blamed for the radical statements that were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, somebody wanted to cut off parts of your territory. Susanne Woodward from the Brooking Institution, an institution of high renown throughout the world, she says: "Smashed stores fronts, fire bombs thrown and harassed and arrested potential Serb leaders. In many parts of Croatia Serbs were expelled from jobs because of their nationality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can call her to give evidence if you want. Yes. Was there an atmosphere, Mr. Mesic, to cause the Serbs to have fear at this time or is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an exaggeration to say that there was an atmosphere of fear, but that there were improper and inadmissible statements, that is a fact. Also there were dismissals that were wrong; however, people took those who dismissed them to court and they won those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean those 100,000 Serbs who fled Croatia already in 1990, they won these cases for their own jobs; is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused is a lawyer, and he knows that only a person who is a plaintiff can win a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we heard your own statements of a few minutes ago about those murders, what kind of rule of law you had. We're going to hear others later as well. I assume that you're not joking now when you're referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time has come to move on from this sort of argument, which doesn't assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mesic: Do you remember the statement made by the famous artist Edo Murtic in Novi Liste [phoen], a daily from Rijeka, made in June 2000? I'm quoting him: "I remember how a few months prior to the elections in 1990" - he is referring to his conversation with Tudjman - "how he came to me quite delighted, believing that he would turn me into his Augustincic. He thought that we would now do what the Ustashas and Pavelic did not do in 1941. He said that he would send 250.000 Serbs packing away and the remaining 250.000 would be killed." So these are your own newspapers. It's not a Belgrade newspaper. This is Edo Murtic, a famous artist, painter, a well-known intellectual. Do you remember that statement of his about this conversation before the elections in 1990? And I quoted Susan Woodward a few minutes ago and she is referring to the atmosphere before 1990, before the elections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can deal with the conversation by -- or comments by the artist which has been referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The artist Edo Murtic is a friend of mine, by the way, but I do admit that I haven't read that particular statement of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please: I'm just going to briefly quote the newspaper Feral Tribune on the 21st of April, 2001, autumn 2001, there was a hunt against the Serbs in 1991. It says: "Mercep's killers were killing Serbs en masse in Pogracka [phoen], Puljane [phoen], they were taking people out of their homes in Zagreb and they were trying them but firing bullets into their heads. Norac Oreskovic and others applied similar methods when dealing with the innocent Serbs of Gospic. Spectacular Crystal Nights were organised in Zadar during which tens of houses were destroyed whose inhabitants had the wrong chromosomes." Is that correct, Mr. Mesic? Is that what the Croatian newspaper Feral Tribune said or did this Croatian newspaper lie when they said that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were crimes, and I always asked for them to be investigated and the perpetrators to be punished. Croatia did not have sufficient rule of law, and after all, that is how I won the election, because I have been calling for true rule of law in Croatia. Crimes were committed and perpetrators should be brought to justice. But that is no reason for destroying Dubrovnik, for destroying Vukovar, for destroying Croatian cities. Criminals should be prosecuted, but towns should not be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Perpetrators should be prosecuted, perpetrators should be tried, but the only question is: Who criminals were. Who were the criminals? That's the only question. And criminals should certainly be prosecuted and brought to justice, certainly. So that is the whole point. That is the inversion that was made, Mr. Mesic; isn't that right? You are testifying here that I was the one who broke up Yugoslavia and you were in favour of Yugoslavia and any child in Yugoslavia knows --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we can reach agreement on one thing very quickly here. I am not the person on trial here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's time, Mr. Milosevic. Half past. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now that you weren't speaking the truth a moment ago when we were discussing an issue and questions about the people who were fighting in Bosnia who were not volunteers. And when I asked you about your nephew, who was also in Bosnia, a Croatian soldier there, and he was not a volunteer. He was born in Slavonia so he was not from Bosnia either and had nothing to do with Bosnia, and you said that that was not true, not correct; isn't that so? Now take a look at (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is, so we've got it, is this in -- not in Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it isn't. It's in the other case, the other trial, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I was talking about. All right. But this is what it says here. May I read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you told an untruth a moment ago. You even said that your nephews were too young, whereas here in this transcript from your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. testimony which was given under oath, you are saying something quite different, in fact. Is that right, Mr. Mesic, or is it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My two nephews live in France, and two of them live in Belgrade. And during the war, they were minors. It is a relation of mine, a distant cousin. The interpretation of that was probably erroneous. Who said that -- who told me he was in Bosnia. That is what he told me and that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- I didn't want to interrupt that last exchange, given that it had started, but any further reference to protected testimony should itself be given in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see why this should be given in private session, Mr. May, when I am making no mention here of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- what it refers to, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Those are the Rules. Any reference to private-session matters should be in private session. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see that I have infringed upon your procedure in any way by having brought that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you were asked by a representative of the accused, did you as a speaker take any steps for this matter to be investigated? Because of course [In English] It is the assembly's responsibility regarding the use of the army outside its border. Did you form a commission? Did you put this issue on agenda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't, please. I don't want to waste time. I won't carry on with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when weren't you speaking the truth, Mr. Mesic: Now or then, when you made that statement which was under oath again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his explanation. If there's anything you want to add, Mr. Mesic, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The direct question was whether my nephew was there, and I said no. A relative, a relation of mine, was, which means that individuals were there who were not born in Bosnia. But apart from that one individual that I did know, I wasn't able to ascertain who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, whether you say nephew or relative or distant cousin or whatever I read out here, that's what it said, so there can be no dilemmas there or confusion. Let's move on. Is it true that in your presence Tudjman said that at the end of the war there would be 5 per cent of Serbs in Croatia, by the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he said. He said that was his assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that he said that Tudjman thought that the 1938 solution for Croatia was the best one when it was the banovina of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Tudjman's position that as Vojvodina had been attached to Serbia, and it was never under Serbia, even during World War II, Vojvodina was under the main staff and headquarters of Croatia because Serbia did not have one. And he therefore considered that Avnoj, the anti-fascist World War II council had made a mistake when to Bosnia-Herzegovina as a historical Croatian province had not been envisioned as autonomous province within Croatia. So that position was one that he always stood by, and he considered that Bosnia-Herzegovina had to be a whole, a whole entity, and that it must be within the frameworks of Croatia. But Avnoj, the anti-fascist council, did not take that into account. However, in the electoral campaign, he stated the facts and said that Croatia represented an oblong role with one section cut off. But in that way, he did not move any proceedings to put that right and to ask for alien territory to be attached to Croatia. After he returned from Karadjordjevo, he said that Croatia was to receive the banovina borders plus Cazin and Bihac, Kladusa, and he said, as Milosevic had told him, he said: "Listen, Franjo." That's what he said. You take Cazin, Kladusa and Bihac. I don't need that. That is what we refer to as Turkish Croatia. That's what he told us. Now, whether that was what actually took place, the accused knows that better himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course there was no discussion about carving up Bosnia. We have already had that discussion here. But your explanations are becoming relevant for you. So to recap: You weren't telling the truth with respect to the presence in Bosnia, and later on I am going to call evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. The witness has said he's telling the truth. Now, don't misrepresent the evidence. If you've got a question, you can ask it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we differ because of the translation in your transcript, where it says nephew, and he says relative or distant cousin, whereas otherwise there is no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, to get back to what you were just saying, that you had no intentions of any kind, Globus, the paper, this is a special edition, November 1, 1999, which says the following: "Tudjman was in Canada, paid a state visit to Canada in 1988 and 1989 [As interpreted] -- 1998 and 1999, and dovetailed concepts, first that Croatia had to be independent and autonomous, and so on and so forth. Third, that the Serbs must be brought to the level of a national minority, which meant that Croatia should have been more or less ethnically pure. And fourth, if there are Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the extent that they cannot all be expelled to Serbia, all that remains is to carve up Bosnia-Herzegovina, which will ensure pure Croatian regions and certain restructuring, and this would be joined onto an ethnically pure Croatian state." Isn't that right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is something that can be read in Globus about a plan that was dovetailed in 1988 and 1989 [As interpreted] in Canada with the Ustasha émigrés. Do you know at all about that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that plan whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, on the basis of what you were saying a moment ago, is it true and correct that Tudjman considered the territories that belonged to the 1938 banovina, that it should be annexed to Croatia? Is that what he thought? Is that right or not? Annexed.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that that was what Milosevic had proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm speaking about something else now. I don't want to show you the transcript once again, but you can look at the transcript from that same trial where you testified and the number of the transcript line is 7130. But to avoid having to go into private session, I just want to jog your memory and tell you that you did speak about the subject at that particular time. And just as like a moment ago, when you challenged the fact that Tudjman thought that for Croatia the best solution would be the 1938 banovina solution, also from your testimony, on page 7129 and 7130, you said what you said. So tell me now: Is it true that the HDZ party for you was an extremist nationalistic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this line of questioning is to be of any value at all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If this is to be of any value at all, the following thing should happen: The Chamber will have to go into private session, not because itself necessarily wants to. It simply that this was protected evidence of another Chamber and we don't have rights to do anything else. Second, the transcript will then have to be examined properly with the witness being in a position to read it and the Chamber being able to see the full context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment I do not wish to go into private session. It cuts up the cross-examination, makes it very difficult for everybody else to follow. If there is a significant point here, no doubt our attention can be drawn to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I simply also then ask that the accused reminds me, or through the Chamber, of what page he says its was on which the first reference was to be found. He says 7266 but it doesn't match my page numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's the note we have, 7266. Mr. Milosevic, you will have -- if you want to quote from the transcript, if there's any significance in what was said earlier, do you want to quote from the transcript, we have to go into private session. Those are the rules which we have to follow. Now, if we can avoid doing that, we should do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. May, but it is not proper and correct that the public should not be able to see this, that Mr. Mesic, for the most part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter about that. It is the Rules which we have to follow. This was private session evidence, therefore it should be dealt with in private session. Now, do you want to ask anything more about that transcript or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll ask him something about -- something else from the transcript in the Dokmanovic trial, where he wasn't a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the HDZ is an extremist nationalistic party which introduced a uniform, unilateral way of thought that captured people in this way? Is that what you think? And you expressed words to that effect in the Dokmanovic trial, where you were not a protected witness. The transcript page is 1714 in the testimony against him, and that is where you made a statement to that effect. You said that that was your opinion later on, not straight away, not from the very outset. So when did you come to think that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a moment. In order that the witness can deal with this properly, have we got a copy of the transcript, Mr. Nice? First of all, have we got a copy of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Secondly, can the witness follow it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's in English, I'm afraid, so he probably can't follow it, because his English is not probably at the level to deal with that. But we have a copy for Your Honours if Your Honours haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We, we have it here. Mr. Mesic -- I'll deal with it. Mr. Mesic, what is being put to you in the passage which the accused is asking you about is counsel says, counsel Mr. Fila, put: "We read that for you the HDZ is an extremist nationalist party, a hindrance to democracy which introduced a single way of thinking and which robbed the people. Is that what you really meant?" And you replied: To look at this in terms of the period -- time period Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. involved. "Okay," said witness. "Have you said something like this?" And you replied: "The statement of yours calls for clarification, namely, when the HDZ was established first, when I was its member, when its programme was elaborated, that was a party that was in favour of a multiparty system for democratisation of free society. When the balance of political forces in the HDZ changed, I left the HDZ and I became critical of the policy." So counsel then put: That is to say that this statement, obviously referring to his earlier statement, is from the latter period. And you replied: Yes, from the latter period. Now, you're being asked about the comment that the HDZ was or became an extreme nationalist party, a hindrance to democracy, introducing a single way of thinking. Can you help us as to whether you said that, and if you wish to elaborate on it, do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the HDZ was formed, just like the other parties in Croatia, after the socialist model, I wanted to have a multiparty system. That's what I was in favour of, of a contest of opinion of democracy. That's what I wanted. Now, as the threats were coming from Serbia, threats which the accused himself, via his rallies, was sending out to Croatia, and they were coming from Vojvodina, from Serbia, and from Kosovo, the so-called rallies for truth, where it was stated that the people attending the rallies would go as far as Ljubljana and that what they would do was to stop over in Zagreb, topple the government there, and carry on by way of passing. I considered that the HDZ could mobilise in Croatia people for setting up resistance to that kind of policy on the part of Milosevic, and I joined the HDZ because I considered that we would be able to protect the interests of the Republic of Croatia. However, because of the erroneous policy which prevailed later on, or rather, the erroneous policy towards and vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina, the wrong model of privatisation which was seen and the insufficient functioning of the rule of law in the country, the insufficient functioning of the institutions inherent in the rule of law, I left that policy behind. I stepped down from it, because finally I could still go on being the president of the Sabor parliament. I had to take part in that policy and politics. But as I did not agree with the policies, I left the post of president of parliament and joined the opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, you relinquished the post of president of parliament, as you said a moment ago, only after the first quarter of 1994. However, the destructive policy of the HDZ, according to you, began already in March 1991; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. From your agreement in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you ascribe the destructive policy of the HDZ, you date it to March 1991 and you ascribe it to me. Is that so, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
