utterances.text: Well, if you offered the carving up and division of Bosnia, then it is quite true that in part you did take part in the creation of the wrong kind of policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you well know, I never offered a division of Bosnia nor was that our policy. And if you believe I did so, then please show me one detail which would be illustrative of that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the division of Bosnia. It is sufficient that you paid the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is sufficient to read the book written by General Veljko Kadijevic, the Federal Secretary for National Defence, who speaks precisely of the Virovitica-Karlobag-Karlovac border and that you stood behind that border, Mr. Accused. That same person Kadijevic, the Federal Secretary for National Defence, Blagoje Adzic, General Blagoje Adzic, who was the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army, never came to me. They never, ever came to me in the Presidency, although I embodied the Supreme Command. They never came to see me. I insisted -- it was I who insisted on going to see them. They never came to see me. But if you read Boro Jovic and his books and if you read Mamula and his books, if you read Veljko Kadijevic and his books, you will see that the agreements were only and exclusively made with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that is not correct. I don't know what they say in their books. Mamula retired even before the tensions mounted in Croatia, and later on in Bosnia. But I assume that you are a passionate reader of all these various books. But now tell me, please: As you were referring to the HDZ just now, in 1991 it started acting destructively, so how can you put up with this for a full three years, staying in that destructive party for three years as its executive chief, that is, as president of the Executive Board of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The point is something else. I was the president of the executive board of the HDZ. Let me tell you -- just a moment. From the 29th of December, 1991 until the 7th of August, 1992. This is the period in which I was at the head of the Executive Board of the HDZ. The point is that as soon as I saw that the policy was not the policy I had advocated, I could have relinquished it. That is true. However, in Croatia, I would have been seen as someone who refused to face the problems Croatia was facing at that moment, and it would have been thought that I had not done enough to correct the things that were going wrong in Croatia. I hoped that with those who thought the same way I did, I could correct the HDZ policy, that we could win. That is why, with other representatives, or rather, with 23 MPs of the Croatian parliament, I discussed our leaving the HDZ. This was in 1993. In this way, we could have achieved cohabitation. The opposition would have been the strongest in parliament, and HDZ would have held executive power. Things would have been different had we succeeded. But unfortunately, I was not successful. Only 11 MPs followed me, and we had one vote less than we needed to be the majority in parliament. If you want to make a big change, you need to have a critical mass with you. I thought that 23 MPs in parliament would be sufficient. We did not succeed, but I went over to the opposition. So I cannot pinpoint a date and say up to that date the policy was right; after that date, the policy was wrong. There was a continuity of events in politics. When enough things happen, one responds. My response was to try to contribute, in a positive way, to a better climate and a better policy in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was two years after March 1991, when you say that the destructive policy of the HDZ started. You say that to start with the HDZ was a democratic party and so on. In the HDZ platform, which I assume you contributed to, together with the other leaders of the HDZ, you say that the programme is based, among other things, on the teachings of Ante Starcevic. Let me just remind you what Ante Starcevic said -- or rather, wrote about the Serbs. He called the Serbs -- I don't know if this can be translated. I wouldn't be able to translate it. He called them filthy spawn, horrible slaves, people who were fit for the axe, Austrian dogs, inflated bags?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When was this kind of thing written?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ante Starcevic wrote, for example, in 1870, because the witness based his programme on that of Ante Starcevic, who wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're saying that. The witness hasn't said it. Help us with Mr. Ante Starcevic, who wrote 130 years ago. Was your programme based on his writings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I did not create the HDZ platform or programme. It had already been adopted when I joined the HDZ. Secondly, the teachings of Ante Starcevic do not consist of particular statements that he made under various circumstances. Ante Starcevic, who is referred to in Croatia as the father of the homeland, advocated the idea that Croatia had to be independent. He struggled for the independence of Croatia from Austria and Hungary. In essence, he was a liberal. On the basis of Croatian state law, he demanded the independence of Croatia. This is the part of his teaching that I find acceptable, an independent republic of Croatia. This is what was taken from Starcevic. It was also mentioned, and the accused does not mention this, that the programme was based on the anti-fascist tradition of the peoples liberation struggle. The accused omitted this on purpose, on the traditions of the anti-fascist struggle. So the ideas were not taken just from one source, but from all sources contributing to a positive role for Croatia and its citizens. That is why this was referred to in the preamble to the programme. If we are to speak of history, the accused should say what Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic wrote. He was a Serbian writer who said that Serbs are all, everyone is a Serb, that the Croats were nothing but Serbs of Catholic faith, so that all this should be Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is not assisted by the exchange of abuse, particularly abuse a hundred years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the HDZ policy became more radical with time and that elements who found inspiration in the Croatian state during World War II grew stronger? I'm referring to the fascist independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The more attacks were mounted against Croatia and its integrity, more excesses arose, and more and more people referred to the independent state of Croatia. I was against this. I'm still against this policy, because in essence I am an anti-fascist, and those are the ideas I always struggled for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I asked you about what you said about the HDZ, not about what you say about yourself.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's why I left the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, I see that as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, you betrayed Yugoslavia and contributed to its break-up. Then proceeding to betray those with whom you had collaborated to destroy Yugoslavia. I'm referring to the HDZ and Tudjman. I don't know who is next. Is it true that Tudjman wanted that from the very start, when the HDZ was founded, Tudjman linked it up with the right-wing factions in Croatia, which includes those who do not conceal the fact they are Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, before you answer, allegations are made there which you should have a chance to deal with, a series of them. The first is that, as the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, you betrayed Yugoslavia and contributed to its break-up. Did you regard yourself as betraying Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was elected to the Presidency of Yugoslavia, I believed that I would help to resolve the Yugoslav crisis by political means, that I could contribute to avoiding the war. My proposal to the Presidency was that we should adopt a fully confederal system and that the confederation should be given a time limit, three to five years, that the republics should be declared independent, that the republics should be internationally recognised, that they should recognise each other, and thereby be recognised by the international community, and that on the day when the Federation ceased to exist, a confederation be established. Why? Because everyone was dissatisfied with Yugoslavia. Serbia claimed that it was being exploited. Serbia claimed that they were the ones who funded others. Croatia was saying that its hard currency was being siphoned off to Belgrade. If everybody was dissatisfied, why not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. adopt a new model? My proposal was to have a confederation and to establish what tasks the confederation would perform, how much this would cost, and what the key to the budget would be, to the financing of this. Serbia never expressed its view on this proposal. Instead of this, Milosevic proposed a strong federation. That is what happened to Kosovo and Vojvodina, that this should happen everywhere. We could not agree to this. But I was in favour of negotiations. I thought that it was better to negotiate for ten years rather than to wage war for ten days. Some people were in favour of the war option, and Slobodan Milosevic was certainly one of those. But what could I have done in Belgrade? Who could I have influenced? The generals contacted Milosevic, the army executed what Milosevic's regime wanted, the creation of a greater Serbia, because he was saying that the Serbs should remain in one state. That is the part that was to become Yugoslavia and to be taken from Croatia. That's what General Veljko Kadijevic says in his book, and he was the Secretary for National Defence. Therefore, therefore, the army, when it had been made into a Serbian army, when the Croats, the Slovenians, the Macedonians and others had left, when it had become a Serbian army, it was to perform the job of setting up new borders, and the one who was perpetrating that plan was the one who was destroying the Federation. I wanted to search for a political solution through constitutional means. I had two secretaries, an advisor, and a Chef de Cabinet, and they were the only people I could influence. I have to say they were all Serbs. Who else could I have influenced, and how could I have toppled Yugoslavia? Was it I who did it or was it the person who had the Yugoslav army at his disposal, which had been transformed into a Serbian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, that all the peoples of Yugoslavia should live in one state pertained to Yugoslavia and that the Serbs in Yugoslavia lived in one state was one of the reasons why Serbia wanted Yugoslavia to be preserved, and that is the only thing that you can quote me on saying, not anybody else. And you're making this up, just like others have along the same lines. I asked you the following: Tudjman wanted a Croatian state at all costs, and from the very inception of the HDZ, he firmly relied on the most radical right-wing, which consisted of the most drastic Ustasha; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. Increasingly radical elements started joining the party and then I left the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say in your interview to the AIM and the question was why did Tudjman from the very inception of the HDZ so strongly rely on the radical right wing in which there are some clear-cut Ustasha. You say that you were powerless, that these were forces that were more powerful than you and that Tudjman went along with them and that the forces that you represented were different, and you say that he relied on these extremist forces and he believed that they would be his friends in war, and that after the war he would manage to neutralise them. That was your explanation. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question at the very outset. The HDZ was a democratic party and now the question is what this journalist meant by the very outset. Which outset?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You explained that this was from March 1991 after the meeting in Karadjordjevo. That is your interpretation of the situation, and we are not going to dwell on that. However, you did remain in that same HDZ for another three years and now you're attacking it.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1991 until the end of 1992 cannot be three by any kind of arithmetic. So there seems to be some kind of erroneous arithmetic involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that it was Tudjman's view that Bosnia was a mistake, that it was a mistake to make it as a republic after the Second World War and that it should be annexed to Croatia? Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were his ideas, that Bosnia was supposed to belong to Croatia on the basis of a decision that should have been adopted by Avnoj. That's what we discussed, because we were both in opposition, both Tudjman and I were MPs in the Croatian parliament in 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it true that it is precisely in Zagreb that deportations of the population of Bosnia were discussed? Or as you had put it, the humane resettlement of the population and basically this was ethnic cleansing. Is this right or is this not right?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for humane resettlement, that is something that you talked about and all of those who thought that it was necessary to transport Croats from Slankamen into Croatia and Serbs into Serbia. I certainly took no part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. Let's not dwell on this much longer. I asked you whether you had your own views on this, because in the transcript that I refer to, your opinion is quite obvious. You say that any person with common sense would realise that this is ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, humanitarian resettlement is actually ethnic cleansing. That is why your detachments came, Dusan Silni, Arkan's guard. All of them came in order to carry out ethnic cleansing. That is not even humanitarian resettlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, I am referring to your policy, the policy of Croatia. I am not talking about whether anybody from Serbia did any such thing. Because as you know full well, it is only Serbia that kept its ethnic composition over the past ten years, and nobody was expelled from Serbia, not a single house was torched, and nobody was mistreated because of their ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the fact that in Serbia there were 18 camps where there were Croatian citizens and they were fleeing from Seselj, the Croats from Vojvodina were, and they were settling Croat settlements and they were exchanging their houses for Serb houses. That is the so-called humanitarian resettlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know that there was not a single camp in Yugoslavia, or rather, in Serbia, not for Croats, not for anyone, not for Croats, not for Muslims, not for anyone.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia is still looking for over 3.300 of its citizens. Many of them, after Vukovar and after other places where massacres were committed, were taken to Serbia. We have to know that the Yugoslav army, with paramilitary organisations, which, with the approval of the Serb leadership came to Croatia, destroyed Croatian towns. Why was Vukovar destroyed? Why were the citizens of Croatia taken to Serbia from Vukovar? Why were they taken to camps in Serbia? If the president of Serbia does not know that there were camps in Serbia, then that is the problem of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know, for example, that when this propaganda started about the existence of camps in Serbia, that various foreign delegations spoke to me about this, people who came on other business, and they asked me about these camps? And I answered to each and every one of them: Please feel free to take a helicopter that I have here and that is ready. Put your finger anywhere on a map and that's where the helicopter will take you, and you will see that there is nothing of the sort in Serbia. After a few answers that I gave of this kind, one delegation, it was a German delegation, asked to go, then pinpointed the mine in Aleksinac on a map. They went there and the only thing they found was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. You can give evidence to us in due course. Mr. Mesic, do you know anything about Mr. Milosevic's dealings with foreign delegations? Have you seen any reports or heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I do know that the Yugoslav army, together with paramilitary organisations, took out of the Vukovar hospital almost 300 persons and that they were all liquidated in Ovcara, near Vukovar. I also know that citizens who were taken prisoner in that massacre of Vukovar were transported to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that is not correct. Secondly, please take a look at this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are you suggesting happened at Vukovar, Mr. Milosevic, if it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not correct that anyone from Serbia took citizens from Vukovar to Serbia. It is not correct that any policy of Serbia's influenced the intensification of the conflict in the region of Vukovar. What is correct is that it is precisely the armed detachments of the HDZ that barged into people's homes, into villages around Vukovar and took Serbs away, arrested them, and so on. They attacked Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it disputed that 300 persons were taken from the hospital to Ovcara and there liquidated? Is that disputed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have these figures, Mr. May, and I'm not discussing them now. But I shall try to find these facts and figures and see what kind of facts and figures are available. I can claim, though, that no Serbian authorities had absolutely anything to do with this, nor did the Serb authorities cause any kind of ethnic conflicts in Vukovar. Ethnic conflicts in Vukovar were caused by the same people I quoted a minute ago, those who took people out of their homes in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've asked you some questions about that. Now, let's move on to matters which the witness can deal with, in particular, his evidence. Time, as you know, is limited, Mr. Milosevic. We must allow some time for the amicus to ask any questions that they want this afternoon. And any re-examination, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's likely to be some, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could you help about the amicus?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there will be questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you ask for, Mr. Tapuskovic? Can you give us an idea, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard for me to say. I will honour any decision you make, but it seems to me that half an hour would be absolutely indispensable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We may not be able to give you half an hour, I'm afraid, because time is short. We can extend the sitting this afternoon until 2.00, unless the Registry have any difficulty about that. There's another hearing this afternoon, but I anticipate we can sit until 2.00, and we will extend the hearing until then to accommodate as much questioning as we can. But Mr. Milosevic, your time is limited, as you know. So let's move on. If you've got any matters that you want to challenge on what the witness said in his evidence, you should do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, of course I am challenging almost everything that the witness said during his testimony. But I assume that it is clear to you that limiting time for the cross-examination of this witness is quite contrary to the need to ascertain the truth. After all, the other party announced that they would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. examine him for ten hours and then they decreased the number by two and a half times in order to diminish my ability to cross-examine him. However, I am going to use the time that is given to me, and you will have to deal with the fact that you haven't given me enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know that there were 221 camps for Serbs in the period between 1991 and 1996 in Croatia? The five that you refer to in Serbia never existed. And here you have a list of all the 221 camps for Serbs in Croatia, and also a map that shows where they were and how many were in different towns and so on. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that I have been highly critical in terms of the functioning of rule of law in the state of Croatia until the year 2000, the truth is that there were no camps in Croatia. There were abuses, there were crimes. That is certain. However, unfortunately, I did not answer the question that had to do with Vukovar. Do I have to give an answer? I do. Those who carried out liquidations were given decorations and were promoted to the rank of general and other such ranks. They still live in Belgrade and they are wanted by this Tribunal. So I'm not the one who is inventing things. The only persons who were not taken out of Vukovar were those who were liquidated in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, no army could have executed or liquidated anyone. You know full well as a citizen of Yugoslavia until it was broken up and you have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a matter which the Trial Chamber, I suspect, is going to have to determine in due course, and it sounds as though these are matters of argument. So, Mr. Milosevic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, is it clear to you that in that Yugoslav People's Army, there could not have been a single officer who would have issued orders to have innocent civilians executed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is precisely the point, which is purely one of argument and nothing else. Now, have you got further questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have an enormous number of questions left, but I have a present for Mr. Mesic, a map of camps for Serbs from 1991 to 1996, with a list of all camps according to different towns. 221, to be exact. When he goes back to Croatia, let him check that out and then he can give an answer to this question, because obviously he cannot give an answer now. Could you please have this map shown on the ELMO. 221 camps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need that, because this simply is not true. There were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just let us see. What is this document that you're producing, Mr. Milosevic? Where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The committee for collecting information on crimes against humanity that were committed and violations of international law, published in Belgrade the 5th of February, 2001. I was no longer president of Yugoslavia then. On the 5th of February, 2001. It is the committee for collecting information on crimes committed. This is a map with all the camps and a list of all the camps in Croatia. However, in all fairness, in Bosnia-Herzegovina there were 536.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not rank first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have this put on the overhead projector so it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For what it's worth, this document may be put on the overhead projector, the witness can look at it. He probably hasn't seen it. It can be shown to the Prosecution. And then, Mr. Milosevic, if you want to prove it, that is, you want it exhibited, then you can prove it yourself when you call your evidence. Yes, Mr. Mesic, you can -- Don't interrupt. Mr. Mesic, just have a look at that, see if there's anything that you can say about it or not. You've heard where it comes from, you've heard what it purports to be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatia did not have any camps, but I do repeat: There were illegal acts, there were abuses, there were crimes, and what I'm asking for is that every crime should be investigated and the perpetrators punished. I am struggling for individual guilt to be established. I don't want any collective responsibility. This has nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the Prosecution have that document and then it can be returned to the accused. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that among the generals that you refer to, that they took part in operations in Bosnia, were Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down. The interpreters could not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down. Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some generals themselves said that they were in Bosnia, but they said this subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, subsequently. Petkovic, Roso, you say that they were not there?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying anything. I'm just saying that they did not say then, that they said afterwards that they had been in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you said that the decision on the ethnic cleansing of Muslims was not formally passed but that it was carried out. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I imagine it is understandable that if everybody leaves a village and that they were forced to leave a village, that that is ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as far as Pero Markovic is concerned, the mayor of Capljina, you said that he carried out ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, how does it help? How is it relevant whether an individual carried out ethnic cleansing in Bosnia? To deal with an indictment? What you must understand is that attacking others is not a form of defence, and therefore the relevance is strictly limited. Now, what is under investigation in this trial is the activities which are alleged in the indictment. For you to attack the others is no defence and of little, if any, relevance. Now, have you got anything else you want to ask this witness about his evidence as opposed to allegations that you want to make about others? No doubt this institution has investigated and will investigate those allegations against others, but it's of no assistance to this Trial Chamber to make allegations about the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats in 1992 and 1993 when we're dealing with crimes alleged to have been committed by you and others in Croatia strictly, but also in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what I'm bearing in mind is precisely the profile of this witness. As for everything that happened, he accuses me, first and foremost, then he accuses his former president and his former political party, and his own generals, and he was the one who gave them instructions, and he also accuses his own politicians, the ones that he gave instructions to, in order to protect himself from responsibility, which is vast, both in terms of the break-up of Yugoslavia and everything else that he is now accusing the HDZ and Tudjman and other factors of, under this slogan that this is the rule of law that he favours and that that's what he's struggling for. And until 1994, what, he did not struggle for the rule of law then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The accusations which a witness might make are not relevant. It's his evidence which he makes and it's on that which you must concentrate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am testifying about the facts that I know about. I cannot testify about those that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. Who destroyed the bridge in Mostar? Is it correct that it was destroyed by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not going to allow the question. Move on to something else, Mr. Milosevic. You really must deal with this witness's evidence, not a generalised attack upon the Bosnian Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, are the words correct by Imre Agotic, your military ally, that were published in Zagreb that the greatest crimes were performed when they were taking over the terrain, that is to say, when the MUP of Croatia and the police were taking over the terrain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which terrain are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic -- yes. Another question, and move off this topic. Move on to something more relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. As you say that you didn't meddle and interfere in this, is it true that you, as a high-ranking functionary of the HDZ, personally went to Bosnia-Herzegovina and replaced Stjepan Kljuc from the post of HDZ head in Bosnia? Is that true or is it not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not replace him. I went there as an HDZ official, but that has nothing to do with this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it does have very much to do with this trial, because it testifies to your direct involvement in the events in Bosnia, for which you accuse me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, since you've been asked.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina was under the influence of the HDZ of Croatia, because ultimately the HDZ was the one that founded it. And when the first president was replaced, the first president of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then what we had -- what had to be done was for a new HDZ president for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be elected. This could only be done at a party congress. But that party congress was not scheduled. A Presidency meeting was scheduled. President Tudjman asked me to go to Siroki Brijeg, which is where the HDZ Bosnia-Herzegovina was meeting at the time, to intervene in this method of replacement of Stjepan Kljuc, who at the time was president of the HDZ Presidency for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I got in touch with some people. I went to Siroki Brijeg. I spoke to people there, and they told me that they supported Stjepan Kljuc. What I said to them was the following: Kljuc, it is my task that he be replaced, but that I talked to people and that he would be given a vote of confidence if he tenders his resignation. However, what he did was indeed tender his resignation, irreversibly, and went to Sarajevo. Before doing so, he asked me: "How are you going to explain that away to Tudjman? That is to say if I am given a vote of confidence, how are you going to explain that to Tudjman?" And I said: "Well, I'll say the majority was in favour of not accepting your resignation and you will remain the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. president of the HDZ party." And then he became afraid. He was afraid for his own survival. He got into his car and left Siroki Brijeg for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it true that the various decisions which refer to Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only the one you mentioned a moment ago, among others, was taken by people in Zagreb, such as Vice Vukojevic from Zagreb? Was Vice Vukojevic a member of the Croatian Sabor or parliament?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the Croatian Sabor, and he did appear in uniform, in HVO uniform. Otherwise, his origins are from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I said to President Tudjman that I didn't like what Vice Vukojevic was doing. I criticised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You talk to Vukojevic and he said that they had shot people. Is that right or not, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can find that in the transcript, 7063.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said something else. I said something else. And please don't distort what I and he said. He said that in the battle for Prozor, the place called Prozor, a lot of Muslims had lost their lives, and I asked him whether anybody had been killed on the Croatian side or perhaps wounded. He said no, and that was all. I didn't have any further conversation with him because I didn't think that you could have people killed on one side and nobody even wounded on the other. And I never spoke to him again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were angry with him, were you, because of that, because you in fact ascertained that crimes had been committed, but you didn't take steps at all. All you did was to be angry with him and you never spoke to him again.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused is well aware of the fact that this was Bosnia-Herzegovina, their territory, and that I wasn't able to undertake anything there. He knows that full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there were many members of the Croatian parliament who went to Bosnia, many Croatian MPs who went to Bosnia during the war, not only Vice Vukojevic but others too, wearing uniforms, to take part of the war there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt now because there's a real danger of this trial being totally sidelined about matters which were not part of the witness's evidence, and that is namely the conflict in Bosnia between the Croatians and the Muslims. Now, Mr. Kay, you mentioned a matter earlier, and on the grounds that this might be relevant in terms of credibility of the witness. But obviously the Trial Chamber must keep the matter within bounds. The witness's evidence is essentially about Croatia, although I'm aware that Bosnia, of course, is also subject of an indictment and to some extent his evidence may be relevant to that. The question is to what extent is the accused entitled, if at all, to examine matters which at the moment appear to have no bearing at all on the issues which the witness raised or indeed the issues in the trial. This is a serious matter because clearly if he's going to follow the same approach which he used before, which was to use cross-examination as a vehicle to make allegations against the other side, to what extent is he entitled to do that, do you submit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He's entitled to attack the credentials of this particular witness, who has maintained during his direct examination that he was only seeking to enforce the rule of law and was not a party taking part in hostilities within the region. Plainly, the accused disagrees with that and is attacking the knowledge of this witness as to what were the real events within the region and the participation of himself and his political party within those events. One appreciates that there is a time limit on a witness giving evidence, and that is the real issue here for the accused. Time spent on matters that are not productive of his defence to the indictment obviously can cause him to be in difficulty in putting forward a defence to the charges. But in many respects, we believe he is aware of those issues. They have been sufficiently in force during the trial, and attempts have been made by the amicus to ensure that he does put his case and is given an opportunity to do so. In many respects, where the subject of the Trial Chamber's ruling here in relation to timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the point is that he obviously is entitled to test the witness's credibility by asking about matters relating to Bosnia, but the real issue is: How far can he go down that road? It would seem to me that once he has put a question in relation to a particular matter touching on Bosnia and he has received an answer on that, then he should move on to another issue. In that regard, he would have been allowed to test credibility in relation to that matter, but I think the issue being raised by the Presiding Judge is that apparently he goes too far down the road, and that tends to take us into areas that are not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A helpful way may be to just make the point here that the Trial Chamber is aware of the matters that have been put in issue by the accused, that the Trial Chamber is aware that he has put in issue various aspects of this witness's evidence, so that any reinforcement of that fact is not further necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's been said. You know there are time limits. There is a question of how far you can continue to deal with matters which are purely peripheral, and bear in mind, as has been said, that the Trial Chamber realises quite well what you're putting in issue and the challenges you make to the credibility of this witness. You should therefore deal with any matters which you think are important, which you might not otherwise be able to do so because of time, as early as possible. Now, you are subject to time limits, and there will be another seven minutes and then we'll have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understood that in addition to the time constraints and limits that have seen to be precipitously come to the fore in the case of this witness, that I do have at least until the close of business today. I think that is a minimum. But I think that it would be in order if you were to give me a little more time, if you were really to take into account the quest for truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have in mind the time limits taken by the Prosecution. You should have roughly similar. You can have until 20 minutes before the end, and that means 20 minutes to 2.00, and that is to allow the amicus some time and also time for some re-examination. I'm afraid both of those will necessarily have to be curtailed. Yes, let's move on. You've heard the points that have been made about Bosnia and the events there in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You were the president of parliament and presided over a meeting on the 24th of September, 1992, at which the deputy public prosecutor in Gospic Djoko Kalanj was relieved of duty, and you also knew that Kalanj was killed already in October 1991. You relieved him of duty then because he didn't turn up for work, although he had actually been killed 11 months before in the crimes that had taken place and that are well known. Is that right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is notorious insinuation. Neither did I know that Mr. Kalanj had been killed, nor did I know what had happened to him at all. As president of the Sabor, I received a proposal from the committee to nominate and relieve of duty members of parliament, and I put the proposal to the vote. I later learnt that that particular individual had in fact been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was killed first by those authorities of yours and then he was relieved of duty for not turning up to work in the morning. Is that a material fact, regardless of your knowledge or awareness or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered the question. Move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you were saying that Josip Tito was an integral factor, but already in 1971, you worked towards the downfall of Yugoslavia when the integral factor lead Yugoslavia and he was a Croat to boot. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, this is notorious insinuation. My positions were one thing. Croatia was not on a footing of equality because it was not able to handle the foreign currency that it earned. So we didn't have clean bills and arithmetic. And what I took part in was in financial fairness with respect to Croatia and Yugoslavia and to clear up the accounts. Now, what I was taken to task for, I talked about yesterday. I still consider that Tito, with his charisma, was an integral factor. He was a politician who stood at the head of Yugoslavia at the time when Yugoslavia played a positive role, that is to say during the conflict between East and West. He created the non-align movement with others, and that was a positive factor, and that was why many people in the world were very sentimentally well disposed towards Yugoslavia. And the accused knew that full well, and that is why he said he was fighting for Yugoslavia at a time when he was using all the resources at his disposal to ensure its breakdown. And I was not tried because I jeopardised or in any other way threatened or claimed that Tito was not a factor of integration. Yes, he was, but he had left the world arena. He was a product of his time. He was a communist. He was a Bolshevik. All that is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, as we are talking about the atmosphere that prevailed and you say that it was Belgrade that stirred up the Serbs, is it true that in 1990, in February, at Vatroslav Lisinski hall in Zagreb at the HDZ rally, 32 Ustasha émigrés from a number of countries in the world attended that rally and meeting? I hope that is not being challenged.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the first congress of the Croatian Democratic Union was being prepared, talks were held between the HDZ leadership and the then Secretary for Internal Affairs, or rather, the Minister of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Croatia. We discussed with him this matter and ascertained that some people would be coming who perhaps could be held responsible for breaking the law. What was said was that everybody could come who had not been tried as a war criminal, that they would be able to come freely, to come and go, that they would be given free passage and would not be prosecuted if they were not in fact war criminals. That was the agreement that was reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that, quite contrary to that Croatian extreme nationalism, that the Serbs in Croatia at those first elections came out in vast majority in favour of the League of Communists of Croatia led by Racan and not for some kind of Serb party or any idea from Belgrade or policy put forward from Belgrade? Do you know that 21 members of parliament in the Sabor, that they had them -- that they were on the list of the League of Communists of Croatia? Do you know about those 21, that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDP went to the elections, the party for democratic change, and not the Communist Party. Many Serbs were elected, that's true. I don't know their exact number. Some of them were on the SDP democratic change party list, others were elected from amongst the other parties, as well as the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party. So they were members of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question to you was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn. You can ask the question after the adjournment. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it clear that the very fact that in all the areas inhabited by Serbs, 90 per cent of them were in favour of Racan's party, in which the Croats were in the majority, that this shows that they were in favour of a federal Yugoslavia and that they wanted to remain a state building and constituent nation in Croatia? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the referendum at which the citizens of Croatia voted on whether they wanted an independent Croatia or to remain in Yugoslavia, 94.17 per cent voted in favour of independence. Among them were Serbians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that show that the issue is something else and that the HDZ, which won the elections with extreme nationalist views, was a clear message to the Serbs as to what awaited them?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that some messages were unacceptable, but there was no reason for Serbs to fear. Excesses started when emissaries arrived from Serbia and when the leadership in the municipalities where the majority Serb population said that they were in fact ostensibly in favour of Yugoslavia but they were in fact in favour of the creation of a greater Serbia. They had been deceived and manipulated, because in the end the programme, the plan to create a greater Serbia failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know there was no such plan, but who actually contributed to the anxiety of the Serbs and to their concerns? I think that without doubt, you are one of those mostly responsible for that. For example, in the summer of 1990, on the occasion of your visit to Gospic, you said, I quote: "The Serbs from Croatia, while they are ploughing Croatian land, pray to God that rain might fall in Serbia. Lets the Serbs go to Serbia but take with them only as much land as they brought when they arrived on the soles of their shoes." Is that what you said, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what you think of me and what I do. That is completely immaterial to me. The quotation is incorrect. The accused put together two things that I said. What I said was, first, that Croats -- that Serbs in Croatian should not plough land in Croatia while praying to God that it might rain in Serbia. This was my response to those who wrote graffiti on walls in Croatia saying this was Serbia. It was not Serbia. It was Croatia, and that's what I wanted them to know. I wanted them to know that they could not engage in implementing such a policy. The second thing I said was that when Serbs arrived in Croatia, they were not carrying Serb land on their shoes to transform Croatian soil into Serbian soil. I wasn't saying anything about what they should take away with them. What I said was that they had not brought Serbia with them on their shoes. Just as the Croats who went to live in Austria, in Burgenland, did not take Croatia with them on the soles of their shoes. They took it with them in their hearts. But they are loyal citizens of the Republic of Austria, although they are aware of their ethnic origins, their Croatian origins. So my message to the Serbs was that Croatia was their homeland, that they can love their former country, but that they should be loyal citizens of the Republic of Croatia. In fact, my message to them was that we wanted them in Croatia, not that they should leave Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the Serbs in Croatia cannot be compared to my grant workers in Austria? The Serbs lived in Croatia on their own land for several centuries. They did not arrive there as migrant workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think the accused misunderstood me or at least pretends to have misunderstood me. Several centuries ago Croats emigrated from Croatia to Burgenland. They were aware of their Croatian origins but they are loyal citizens of the Republic of Austria. They have their municipalities, territories. They are protected by legislation of the Republic of Austria as a national minority. This was my message to Serbs, that they should be loyal citizens of the Republic of Croatia and not listen to the emissaries of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mesic, but at the pre-election rally that was held in Gospic on the 2nd of March, 1990, which was attended by about 15.000 Croats, and because it was raining, many of them were carrying umbrellas, you said there: When we Croats establish our own state, all the Serbs in it will fit under a single umbrella. This rally was held on Nikola Tesla Square in Gospic. Is this correct, Mr. Mesic, or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. I don't know who attributed these words to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have time to prove this because my time is limited.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will never be able to prove it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will prove it, just as I will prove that you worked for the military counter-intelligence service and many other things that you denied here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Slovenian TV show on the 8th of November, 1995, on a private television station, you said that Mr. Genscher and Pope John Paul the second, with the support they gave to the break-up of Yugoslavia, contributed the most to the break-up of this country. You said: I wanted to transmit the idea of the collapse of Yugoslavia to those who could influence its fate the most, Genscher and the pope. Genscher made it possible for me to contact the Holy See and they agreed to the total break-up of Yugoslavia. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to ask the accused not to make me laugh, because this is a place where we should be serious. I never spoke about this. I never spoke of Croatia or Slovenia breaking up Yugoslavia. It was Slobodan Milosevic and his regime who are working for that. I was speaking of independence. When Yugoslavia lost its integrating factors, when it became quite clear that the executive council, the Supreme Court, the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the constitutional court, had become blocked, that no institutions were functioning, it was quite clear that such a federation, such as it was, was untenable. And when it became quite clear that Croatia had to seek a way out, and this way out could only be in independence, we had to look to those who would support our right to independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, at a press conference in Belgrade, in the press centre, in December 1990, you said that there were no misunderstandings in Yugoslavia since the HDZ, or rather, that these misunderstandings did not begin when the HDZ came to power in 1990 but that they started, in fact, in 1918. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. The misunderstandings did not arise when the HDZ came to power. The misunderstandings date further back. If necessary, I can explain that. The Austro-Hungarian monarchy could not be preserved according to the same model in which it had existed. The Austrian emperor, Franz Josef did not understand what was going on on the territory of this great empire. Franz Ferdinand thought that on the territory of the former empire, a personal union should be established, just modelled on the commonwealth, so that parts of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy should become independent and that a personal union should be established. This was the threat to greater Serbian policy which existed then, because they knew that the ambitions to break up Bosnia and Herzegovina would no longer exist if this came to be. Because from Garasanin onward, greater Serbian policy wanted Serbia to expand across the River Drina. If the peoples and the states on the territory of the empire became independent, Serbia would no longer be able to expand its borders across the River Drina. That is why the organisation called "the Black Hand" decided to assassinate Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've probably exhausted that topic in 1918.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear, Mr. Mesic, from what you said - and here I include your presence in Siroki Brijeg in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for those who don't know where Siroki Brijeg is - where the Croatian historical rights in Bosnia were put forward, Boban and you and most other participants advocated this, and it was only Kljujic who advocated Bosnia as a whole, as an entity, which is why he was replaced. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've already dealt with Mr Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when you parted ways with Tudjman - while you were implementing this policy, you advocated the same views - you said that Croatia was a twilight zone, that it was approaching the model of Paraguay that it was a risk zone, and that the rules that applied there were --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain again. I said that Croatia -- in Croatia the rule of law did not apply, that there were abuses, that there were crimes, that tycoons appeared who were destroying the Croatian economy, which is why I parted ways with that policy. I demanded that Croatia function as a state in which the rule of law applied, and I demanded that Nazi and fascist symbols which here and there appeared in Croatia should be done away with. Today, Croatia is discussing a law, a bill, in parliament on banning Nazi symbols and punishing those who put forward such symbols in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mesic. Are you claiming that you yourself did not personally contribute to the development of this fascist climate towards the Serbs when you were one of the top leaders of the HDZ? Later on you call this a twilight zone, but did you contribute to its creation or not? Do you consider yourself responsible, co-responsible, for the creation of this twilight zone and the expulsion of the Serbs from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is entirely wrong. I was an anti-fascist from my youth. My whole family was on the Partizan side. Not a single member of my family was on the other side. Eleven members of my family were killed fighting on the anti-fascist side. I am a convinced anti-fascist, and I find all this distasteful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that you criticised Tudjman for signing the Vance-Owen Plan when representatives of the UN were deployed in the territories where there was a conflict - these were the UN-protected areas - and you criticised him because Croats could not enter the Krajina until a political solution was found? Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I criticised many decisions made by President Tudjman and supported others, depending on the point in time. When Tudjman suggested that a referendum on Croatian independence be held, I felt that the elections had been enough for citizens of Croatia to show what they wanted. I thought it was enough. But Tudjman said: No. Let's have a referendum. I opposed the referendum, but later on I saw that in that case Tudjman had been right. Sometimes I supported Tudjman, sometimes I did not. But I cannot discuss now every instance where I supported him or not, because I think this is of no interest to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In agreement with Tudjman, when you, the prime minister, you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. issued a decision on the withdrawal of the reserve forces of the police from municipalities, mostly in the Krajina, where the Serbs were in the majority, you remember that, I assume.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is yet another lie and another trick. A decision was made to collect weapons in all municipalities of the Republic of Croatia so that Croatia could defend herself, because the authorities in Belgrade had previously issued a decision that all weapons should be withdrawn from Croatia so that Croatia could be brought to her knees. The Territorial Defence, I have to explain, was commanded by a staff in Zagreb, the staff of the Territorial Defence. The army - that is, the army of the SFRY - was commanded by the General Staff in Belgrade, but both were components of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. We held the opinion that it was improper to withdraw weapons from the Territorial Defence because these weapons were protected in Croatia. However, evidently the regime of Slobodan Milosevic and his subordinates felt it was in their interest to disarm Croatia and to arm the rebellious Serbs in order to implement the plan that General Kadijevic also speaks about, and that is the establishing of the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag border. I know the accused does not like this, but these are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to dislike here. These are not facts but your political opinions, Mr. Mesic, because you have failed to put forward a single fact here. Along with a decision to collect the weapons from the Serb areas in late July, you also made a decision to establish the National Guard Corps. This was a paramilitary formation. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to remind the accused that, on the one hand, there were illegal paramilitary organisations and there were legal paramilitary organisations. The police force is also a paramilitary organisation. They have weapons, they have uniforms, and they have a chain of command. But they are not an army. Croatia adopted a decision that the National Guard Corps be established. Its purpose, in fact, was to be something like the gendarmes in France or the carabinieri in Italy. We wanted to have a unit which could be activated, in case of need, if the vital interests of the Republic of Croatia were threatened. At that time, this was not yet the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This decision of the Croatian government was to have been implemented, first of all, in the area of Lika, where Serbs made up 93 per cent of the population; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did you get this 93 per cent? That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. The majority.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 93 per cent and 51 per cent is a big difference. But as we have heard, the accused no longer stands by the usual kind of arithmetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the political and security situation deteriorated, did the political leadership of the Serbs in Krajina decide to hold a referendum on autonomy? This was in late August 1990.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to respond again, although I have already answered a part of this question: Weapons were collected on the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia, and the referendum was illegal, and Croatia failed to recognise it, did not recognise it, because it was an illegal referendum, and in Croatia law has to be respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 16th and 17th of August, when the police set out toward Benkovac, where 10.000 Serbs had gathered, do you think that this move that you made had anything to do with the reactions of the Serbs and that it was not actually incited by the authorities of Serbia? You said Belgrade -- I mean, when you say "Belgrade," I assume you're referring to the federal organs of Yugoslavia, not to the leadership of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the accused and his regime and his links with the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that a bit later. Did this have anything to do with the reaction of the Serbs, the fact that the police set out to Benkovac, where 10.000 Serbs had assembled? Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police did not set out against anyone. They could only provide security at the rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so they went there to guarantee their security.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that such wrong decisions of yours, to send police to places where people had rallies, in spite of the constitutional right to freedom of assembly, was a wrongful decision which made the Serbs place roadblocks; this was not part of a struggle for a greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this trial I've answered that question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mesic. After this Croatian government was constituted, the one whose prime minister you were, wasn't it clear that at that time the activity of the organised arming of HDZ members started? Is that right or is that not right? Is that being contested too?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was prime minister of Croatia for three months before I went to Belgrade, and on the 17th of August, 1990, the log revolution started. Roads were blocked, roads that were of vital interest to the economy of Croatia. Croatia had to survive, both politically and economically. Who was it who was destroying Croatia then? Was it those who wanted to establish free traffic on Croatian roads or those who were carrying out orders issued by the accused and provoking the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It just so happens that the accused at that time was vacationing in Dubrovnik and heard about this from the newspapers there. But are you trying to say that logs are some kind of offensive weapon, or is it the police that enters settled areas and attacks people? Was anybody ever attacked by a log?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, logs are a very lethal weapon, because they do not allow free communication in Croatia. They do not allow the economy to function. This is a grave attack on the Croatian economy and the Croatian state. Before that, I would really like to hear where this happened, where the police attacked someone so the Croatian roads had to be blocked. I would really like to hear that once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I've given you countless examples - I've presented them here anyway - during 1989 and 1990, many examples. I even quoted your own newspapers to you, about incursions, about arrests, about people being taken away and who are still missing. You know about that. Mr. Mesic, do you think that since at that time you were prime minister, you are the guiltiest person of all for clashes with the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this is nonsensical, I am going to dignify it with an answer. They opted to provoke the Croatian authorities in order to establish the boundary that I refer to. Specifically in Pakrac, there was a conflict between two streams in one police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's taking up my time. He spoke about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've put serious allegations to him. He must be able to answer them. Yes. Go on, Mr. Mesic.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since part of the police station was disarmed, the Minister of the Interior sent reinforcements in and disarmed the attackers. That brought an end to it all. However, the army came into the streets with 20 or 30 tanks, and they purportedly separated the conflicting parties. There were no conflicting parties. There were those who were attacking the police and there were those who were protecting the police. There were no two parties that were clashing. There was not an interethnic conflict there. Nobody was wounded. Nobody was killed. I came to Belgrade. Borislav Jovic, the representative Serbian of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, said that there was a massacre of Serbs in Pakrac, where 40 persons were massacred. I said, "Well, I was in Pakrac yesterday. Nobody was wounded. Where did you read that?" And he said, "In the Titograd daily newspaper of Pobjeda." Now, where is Titograd? Where is Pakrac? They have nothing to do with each other. But it is obvious that this is a scenario. The army was supposed to be brought into the picture to ensure the boundaries that not only General Kadijevic knows of very well but also this accused, Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This accused doesn't, and I do not consider myself to be accused by this false indictment. And since you behaved the way that you behaved, that you behaved in this broad-minded, democratic manner, how is it then possible and why were you the protagonist of a programme that Serbs were supposed to be expelled from the constitution of Croatia as a constituent and state-building people?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia proclaimed its independence. It had its own institutions, it had its own parliament, and it passed laws. I'm not in a position now to interpret why each and every law was passed and in which way and how the constitution was adopted. There is a procedure involved. I don't know in which case I would have to give answers now in respect of a decision that is reached by the parliament of my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A parliament that you chaired. So you believe that you preserved the status of the Serbs that they had according to all previous constitutions. I mean, had you retained that status for them, that they still would have rebelled; is that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Institutionally, no rights of Serbs or of any other ethnic group were violated. I admit that there were some messages that were unacceptable, but they had to be discussed at a table, not by destroying Dubrovnik, not by destroying Vukovar, Skabrnja, Vucine, not Cetekovac, not by massacring people. In that way, not a single conflict can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, as a member of the Presidency, later on you even compounded your responsibility for everything that happened to the Serbs in 1991 and 1992 and later on your responsibility as Croatia's -- as the president of Croatia's parliament, at the beginning of 2000, you stated, on television, that the Croats in 1995, through military actions, that is to say, through storm and flash, in the war for the homeland, that they won a glorious victory. Mr. Mesic, no doubt storm and flash are actions that meant carrying out war crimes and ethnic cleansing, ethnic cleansing of practically all Serbs from Croatia. Do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know that this is not the time to make speeches or try and give evidence, which you're trying to do. Have you got a question to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, I do have a question. If these were glorious actions, why are you saying now that Bobetko should be held responsible if he was doing something glorious, in your words?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The victories in the homeland war were glorious because they made it possible for Croatia to reach each and every part of the Croatian state and to establish the functioning of the institutions of the Croatian state. In these battles, crimes may occur, as always. I am advocating the following: That everybody should be held accountable for what he did. Croatia adopted a constitutional law in cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. I am advocating the following: That everybody should have the right to defence. All suspects should be held accountable before The Hague Tribunal. If these are Croatian citizens, then they should have the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right to defence, maximum defence, implying dignity and respect for everything that everyone did by way of a contribution to the independence of Croatia. But I want each and every citizen to be equal before the law because it is only then that we can expect to realise our strategic objectives and that is to become part of European and Atlantic alliances, which is truly our strategic objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It is my understanding that the expulsion of 250.000 Serbs from Krajina and taking tens of thousands of them out of columns, according to the findings of Commissioner Ema Bonino, and these persons went missing, simply that you are calling all of this individuals crimes and individual actions. The expulsion of 250.000 Serbs and the destruction of thousands of persons who were in these columns. You are calling this individual crimes within this glorious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with this, and it's not clear what relevance this has to this particular indictment. These are events in 1995. Yes let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm concerned if there's to be the time limitation that the Chamber has identified that the accused is simply not dealing with the matters on which evidence has been given, and typically in the last question but two he slid over 1991 and 1992 with an allegation to which the witness was not allowed to give an answer, that being exactly the time of the Presidency, the Rump Presidency, and the other matters that we should be investigating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the question that you say he should have been able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it was where he suggested -- I'll just find it again. He simply suggested that he compounded everything by his behaviour in 1991 and 1992, without putting any particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has dealt with that. Mr. Nice, there is a question of time. We understood that the witness could not be available tomorrow. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The way I expressed it was he was definitely available yesterday and today and that he might be available for tomorrow. I know his original plans were to travel back tomorrow. But the Chamber will of course be in the witness's hands and he'll know better than I, I not having spoken to him yesterday, what his availability now is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, could you help us with this? You've heard about this question of time. Are you available tomorrow at all in the morning or do you have to get back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some engagements tomorrow afternoon, so I could be present in this courtroom for part of the morning tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you be here for an hour, say from 9.00 to 10.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Milosevic, you can have until 2.00 today. You can have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can have a few minutes tomorrow in addition to that, but there must be time for the other parties to cross-examine and re-examine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your interview to the president of the Association of Writers of Croatia, her name is Marica Mikuljan, this is Nova Matica [phoen] number 7, dated 1992, in response to her question how come you wrote a book, you said, inter alia: My original idea was to call the book "How I toppled Yugoslavia." Mr. Genscher suggested that perhaps in Europe, such a title would not be well received. Genscher added that we all contributed to the break-up of Yugoslavia, and that seemed acceptable to me, hence the title of my book. That's what you said. And then in response to her next question, what was your prognosis for the Balkans after the drama was over, you say, inter alia, in your response: Let me conclude. It is logical that if the opponent was declared to be the devil a priori, then his demonic family should be destroyed too, his demonic country and his entire demonic history. Now, this brings us to the following question: Who declared the Serbs in advance a priori to be the devil, the demon? Did you do that on your own or was it the leadership that you were a part of, or was this done in conquered [As interpreted] with Genscher and what is your role in this kind of a priori qualification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with several questions which were bound up there. The first was the quotation attributed to you about the possible title of a book "How I toppled Yugoslavia." Perhaps you can deal with that. And then there was a question about your prognosis for the Balkans. That was the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct that the title of the first edition of my book was "How we toppled Yugoslavia." The second edition was entitled "How Yugoslavia was toppled." I said this in order to make things quite objective, namely, Croatia, Slovenia, and other republics sought a confederal model. Serbia asked for a so-called firm federation. The status quo could not remain forever. That meant that we had to become independent. As the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia disappeared, we all took part in the process, all of us who wanted changes and a confederacy that would have a time limit of three to five years and also those who were toppling the Federation in order to establish a different kind of federation that Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia could not accept. That is why in the second title I tried to make it sound more objective, and the contents show what this book is really about. As for the other part, that is not a proper quotation. I never said any such thing. Who did this and who in this way deceived the accused, I really have no idea.
