utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that you have been saying that I created the so-called Serbian bloc in the Presidency, I assume that before that you should bear in mind that all divisions in the Presidency were created on the basis of political divisions regarding ideas as to what the destiny of Yugoslavia would be, not on the basis of somebody's influence. Is that right or is that not right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is clear that the leadership in Kosovo was toppled and that autonomy was destroyed, that the leadership in Vojvodina was toppled and that autonomy was destroyed there. And also that the leadership in Montenegro was toppled. These three representatives, along with Borislav Jovic, who represented Serbia proper, were the Serbian bloc. It can be seen by how they voted. And also when Borislav Jovic resigned, others also resigned. But Milosevic comes forth immediately. There is no more Yugoslavia, he says. We are not going to carry out the constitution. There are no valid decisions reached by the Presidency for us. And he, as the president of Serbia, who had to come to a session of the Presidency because according to the constitution he would have to stand in for the member of the Presidency from that republic if he were leave, he said that he would not do that. Now, I am really interested in hearing who was it that was toppling Yugoslavia? We wanted a different concept, and that was legal and legitimate. We thought that this kind of Yugoslavia was untenable. Let us work in favour of a model that was tenable. And if it cannot be sustained, then we are going to part our ways in peace, cooperate mutually as the Czechs and the Slovaks do, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, what you said just now is what you said yesterday too, and then you played a video cassette that speaks to the contrary. Because I never said there that there is no Yugoslavia. On the contrary, I spoke in favour of Yugoslavia. And as for this resignation, as I explained at that time, that's what you broadcast, it was a reaction to the fact that the Presidency did not want to pass its own decisions, and that is why the assembly of Serbia refused Jovic's resignation and returned him to his position two days later. And when I said I would not go there instead of him meant that I thought that he should go back there and work there and that his resignation was a reaction to the fact that the Presidency refused to carry out its own decisions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The film that you showed, where did you see that? And you showed me on television. Where did you hear me say that Yugoslavia did not exist any more and all the rest that you said, and that the Presidency was not going to function and Borislav Jovic, the bit about Borislav Jovic? The events showed you otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer this. Can you help us with this, Mr. Mesic, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I didn't show any excerpts. That has nothing to do with me. It is the Prosecution and indictment that calls for that. As far as I'm concerned, I don't much like watching television images of Slobodan Milosevic. That is far from my thoughts. As for the tape itself, we were able to see the tape. Borislav Jovic and Mr. Bucin tendered their resignations and straight away we see the advent of Slobodan Milosevic, who says that he's not going to use his right to represent Borislav Jovic in the Presidency until that man had not attended the assembly meeting and until his resignation was refused. So once again the accused doesn't seem to handle arithmetic too well, and now I can see that he doesn't handle time too well either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, the aim assembly was scheduled. You know that Jovic returned to work in the Presidency following a decision of the Assembly of his republic and that what you're saying is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we're not going on in this way. Let's move on to another topic. You haven't asked questions about any of the documents that were produced. If you want to do that, Mr. Milosevic, you should do so in the 40 or 50 minutes that remain for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best, Mr. May, to deal with that too, but as I was informed only the day before yesterday that the witness would be available two and a half times less than was originally planned, I'm trying to make a selection of the more important issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Mesic, that the political position of Serbia Montenegro was to stand up against Yugoslavia's breakdown? And is it also true that there was no firm federation as you termed it that was proposed by the representatives of Serbia and Montenegro but quite the contrary, that it was a democratic federation that they put forth, a democratic one, a free one, and I'm sure you will recall that, for example, Serbia, at a meeting of the presidents of all the republics, which was held in Sarajevo, supported the proposal by Izetbegovic and Gligorov, offering a loose type of federation, the loosest possible type, but nonetheless a state of sorts and not some kind of what you would call alliance, confederal alliance for a period of five years. So Serbia lent its support to that particular plan, which meant that all the republics would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gain autonomy, but nonetheless would keep them within the realms of a state. What we wanted to do was to preserve Yugoslavia, and that is what neither you or anybody else can challenge. Isn't that right, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the accused has stated precisely what should have been stated. They were against Yugoslavia, opposed to it. They were offering something that Croatian and Slovenia found unacceptable. Therefore, he was opposed to Yugoslavia, the kind of Yugoslavia that existed at that time, and that's precisely what I'm claiming. He was against Yugoslavia. He was opposed to Yugoslavia, and that is why he used the military option and worked towards the breakdown of Yugoslavia, with a military option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How were you able to conclude that we were opposed to Yugoslavia when the entire public knew full well that we were striving only for the preservation of Yugoslavia, and what we said was that that was the best solution for all the South Slav peoples and nobody would have a better life in any other way, and as to freedoms, rights, the independence and autonomy of the republics, they were never brought into question at all?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had we accepted the proposals made by the accused, then I suppose we had the nice kind of time that the Albanians have had in Kosovo and we didn't want to taste the beauties of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. In Croatia you were under some kind of pressure, as far as I understand it, pressure from Serbia, while Yugoslavia was living. I never noted any pressures of that kind. I don't know where you saw them prevalent. Perhaps you could tell me.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this question is nonsense, nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except in tourism, perhaps, because there were a lot of tourists from Serbia coming to the Adriatic Coast. Is it true, Mr. Mesic, that the first division in the Presidency, the first rift, was caused after your statement that you wanted to be the last president of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused has a terribly rich imagination and he seems to be very adept at distorting things. He knows full well what I said on the occasion at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what did you say?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to Belgrade as somebody who had been elected to the Presidency, and my statement, the statement I made, that Yugoslavia in that model, as it stood, could not survive. Everything that happened later on bore out the fact that I was quite right and that we had to find a political solution, because unless we found a political solution, I would be the last president. Not that I wanted to be the last president, but that I would be the last president, and that is in fact what I was. I was the last president of Yugoslavia, through the will of those people who opted for war, who selected the war option, through the will of those who refused to accept a political solution but who gave arms and weapons into the hands of those who were not to blame. They were to blame because they accepted to bear arms. But the person most to blame was the person who supplied them with arms, who put those arms and weapons in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not being challenged that when you took up the position of president, or rather, a member of the Presidency, as a member from Croatia, that you said that Yugoslavia could not survive, and it is not clear to you; you refuse to accept the fact that this was the cause of the rift in the Presidency, statements of this kind on your part, and the fact that these assertions of yours could not be tenable in view of the office you held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What you must not do is to misrepresent the evidence. Now, the witness has answered the question. He's told you what he said. He's told you he blames your government for what happened. Now, I don't think we're going to get much further on that simply arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you know very well, as a lawyer, that every state has a constitution, and that until that constitution is changed, even if it is a bad constitution, that it is in force and holds true nonetheless. And when I say that the statements made by Mr. Mesic, who, according to that very constitution, was elected to perform the function at the Yugoslav level, that is to say, the top Yugoslav level, that this was untenable with that constitution and with the relationship that he had towards Yugoslavia. So what I am saying is that it was he himself and no Milosevic who was the cause of the rift that took place in the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, for example, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have made that point several times. We have heard you. We understand your case. We will deal with it in due course. We will have to make our own minds up about it. Now, time is limited, and you have to concentrate on asking this witness questions, if you've got any, beyond making statements. I suggest you move on to another topic, we having heard both sides on this particular issue about the early days of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, your thesis is that I forced Montenegro not to accept Carrington's plan; right? Is it clear to you that that is just not true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed that anywhere. I never said that the accused had forced Montenegro not to accept Carrington's plan. All I'm saying is that the accused, with the policy he waged, broke down the autonomous Vojvodina and Kosovo and toppled the leadership, which was a legally elected one, in Montenegro, and that he implemented an anti-bureaucratic revolution, as it's called, by which in fact he destroyed Yugoslavia. Because if you destroy the constituent elements of a federation, those component parts - and they were the two provinces - then Yugoslavia can no longer exist either. And that fate, the fate of Kosovo, is something that we did not wish to repeat for ourselves. Let me be quite clear to the very end now. Why didn't the accused fuss over the fact that the Serbs were fleeing from Croatia? Because he needed that critical mass of people to populate Kosovo once he had expelled the Albanians from Kosovo. That is the plan the accused had, to throw out the Albanians and to bring in the Serbs from Croatia to populate the area. That was what he had in his mind: to destabilise Albanian and to destabilise Macedonia as well, because that mass of Albanians coming in would, of course, destabilise those two weak countries. That was his plan, and he counted upon the fact that he would be the factor and element which the international community would seek to calm the region, but the NATO pact stepped in to stop those awful plans of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, your imagination is commendable, but unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- But unfortunately, there are many defects in it. First of all, as regards Montenegro, do you recall that in Montenegro a referendum was held; that is to say, it was not an anti-bureaucratic revolution which engulfed the people and subjugated the people, but there was a referendum at which the citizens of Montenegro stated their views and opted for Yugoslavia? It was not under pressure of any kind. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered that. Everything that was done in that particular region was done through the will -- and that is to say not only the will of Milosevic but on the will of his regime, the toppling of those leaderships. That was what he wanted to do. He held speeches in front of millions. He mobilised the populace. He convinced them that all the Serbs would live in one single state, and obviously when you seize other people's territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Show me that speech of mine. Show me one speech in which I said a single word against Croatia or Yugoslavia. Do you have one single example to show us of that kind?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If you claim that the Serbs in Croatia have the right to self-determination, they then decide, not the Serbs in Croatia but the rebel Serbs. I don't want anybody to think that I am blaming the Serbs in Croatia. No. The greatest portion of Serbs lived in Zagreb, for example. There were more of them living in Zagreb than the entire Krajina region. I'm talking about the insurgent Serbs, those who rebelled and those who wanted to annex Serbia, this to Serbia, and made that decision, and so did Milosevic's regime, led by him, and they put out the slogan of all Serbs living in one state. So those affiliated Serbs too. It is true that Serbia did not pass a decision which would make this legal, but neither were they opposed to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is just not true. That, quite simply, is a lie. And any mention of one state referred to Yugoslavia as a common interest, the common interest of all the Yugoslav peoples. And what I was saying was only in that way would the Serbs be able to live in one country if we preserve Yugoslavia, being that one country. But I also said that all the Muslims could live in one country if we were to preserve Yugoslavia and all the other nations and nationalities scattered around Yugoslavia, and nobody minded that at all. That is the truth, Mr. Mesic, and I think that your memory will serve you well there. But what you're doing now is speculating. But Is what I'm saying right or not?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My memory serves me very well, thank you. Because the accused said if the Slovenes want to leave, let them leave, and you should go as soon as possible. If the Croats want to leave, let them go too. But quite obviously all the Serbs would remain in one single state. In other words, they remain in that state by virtue of their territory, the state that he calls Yugoslavia. I call it an invalid, handicapped Yugoslavia. He terms it otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, from what you have just said, do you in fact confirm the fact that the Serbs in Croatia had lost under your authority the properties and characteristics of a constituent peoples, that is to say, a peoples realising their right to self-determination? Is that what you're bearing out, what you're confirming, the right that they always enjoyed under all the constitutions except the 1990 constitution? Is that what you're confirming by what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs realised their constitutional right to self-determination and formed a republic, the Republic of Serbia. I don't know why -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about the Serbs in Serbia, Mr. Mesic. We're talking about the Serbs in Croatia. It was the Serbs in Croatia who had the status, enjoyed the status of a constituent people in Croatia, and that was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is degenerating into an argument. It doesn't seem it's taking us anywhere. These may be matters which, in the end, we'll have to resolve, but it seems pointless going on about it with this witness. He's made his position clear. You've cross-examined him thoroughly. Now, let's move on to any other topic that you want to examine about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask this: Is it clear to you that when you speak about Vojvodina and Kosovo, that you are in fact speaking about autonomous provinces within Serbia proper, so that therefore you cannot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. transfer this to Slovenia and Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, that same model, because the internal constitutional changes in Serbia were a matter for Serbia to decide, not a matter for Croatia to decide, not a matter for Croatia to decide? Vojvodina is not in Croatia. It is in Serbia. So do you deprive Serbia the right of settling matters in its own house?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the accused is suffering from amnesia once again, because it was the provinces which were a constitutive element of the Federation as well, both of Serbia but also a constituent element of the Federation as well, and that is the portion he deprived them of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quite obviously don't have time to engage in this kind of discussion and debate, but I think that constitutional experts are the ones who are well capable of dealing with these matters, and your distorted concepts of the right of nations to self-determination seems to me to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is all argument and comment. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence in the republics, that it was under the command of the Presidency and the Supreme Command and partly controlled by the republics, where the Territorial Defence of Serbia is concerned, you said, quite incorrectly, that the Territorial Defence units of Serbia waged war in Croatia because the TO of Serbia and Montenegro was exclusively under the command of the army. You say that on page 19 of your statement. How can you say something like that?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence attacked Dubrovnik, together with the rebels from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And with respect to the attack on Croatia, it was the army that was under the command of the General Staff, and together with the Territorial Defence, they attacked Croatian towns and villages. Units of the army arrived from Serbia, and in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia they joined in the attacks and ethnic cleansing. This would have been impossible. It was not possible that no one in Croatia saw that tanks were going from Serbia to Vukovar and other parts of Croatia. This is something that cannot be concealed. Somebody had to see that the army was coming from Serbia to Croatia during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, are you aware of the fact that the JNA was all over the territory of the former Yugoslavia and that therefore Croatia was not a demilitarised republic within the SFRY? When I drew up my demonic plan, as you say, the army then attacked Croatia. No. That was not the case. The army was already in Croatia, just as it was in Serbia and everywhere else in Yugoslavia. Is this clear to you? Is it clear to you that this was all happening when the army was being attacked, when there were clashes with the army, when you were making decisions to drive out the Yugoslav army, not the Serbian army, but the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to bring this to a close. Mr. Mesic, it's put to you, first of all, that the Yugoslav army was already in Croatia, so there was no question of it being brought in, and secondly, that that army was under attack. Would you deal with those two separate points, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that gladly. From the barracks of the JNA, which had by then become a Serbian army because the other nationalities had left it by then, it was this army that was arming the rebels, which is why they were under a blockade, why they were surrounded, so that they could no longer arm those who were attacking and trying to topple the institutions of the Croatian state. Novi Sad is not in Croatia, but it was a Novi Sad corps that attacked Vukovar. Belgrade is certainly not in Croatia, but it was from Belgrade that guards units came to attack Vukovar. Somebody had to have seen this, at least those who, in that aggressive war, promoted those who participated in all this and decorated them. The accused knows very well who these people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, as you know very well, military districts did not coincide with the borders of the republics in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. They are still -- they still do not coincide with these borders in Yugoslavia. For example, in the 2nd -- the 2nd Military District covers a part of western Serbia and yet it's based in Podgorica. So there was a single JNA, a unitary JNA, and you made the decision - and I will tell you exactly when you did that - that it should be driven out of Croatia, that the barracks should be cut off, that electricity and water should be cut for the barracks, that soldiers should be attacked, that they should be beaten up, arrested, and so on and so forth. Are you aware of this or not, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accused knows full well that this is not true, that it's a fabrication. I made no such decisions, nor was I in a position to make them. However, the accused knows very well that the JNA was not allowed to attack Croatian towns, and I would like to know when and where he lodged a protest against this, against Serbian tanks, JNA tanks going to destroy towns in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, when Dubrovnik was being shelled, I was attending a conference with Lord Carrington, together with your president, and then I said that any clash was crazy, that Dubrovnik was a Croatian town. This has nothing to do with what you're saying. But let us go back to your story about the Serbicised army, as you say, because the influence of the Serbian bloc is quite senseless. It doesn't make sense when we are speaking of the JNA. General Kadijevic was half Croat, half Serbian. Adzic was from Herzegovina. Brovet was a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're not giving evidence. You're not giving evidence. It's being put, Mr. Mesic, that you're wrong when you say that the JNA was becoming Serb. In particular, two generals are referred to. Would you like to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not count anybody's blood cells or look at their chromosomes. Individuals did remain because they were afraid for their survival, but that doesn't mean anything. Most of the Croats had left the JNA. All the Slovenians, except for Brovet, and perhaps one or two individuals had left. The Albanians had left the army. The Bosnians had left the army. I'm merely putting forward facts. But exceptions only go to prove the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know that in 1999 or in the year 2000, even then the army of Yugoslavia was not ethnically pure, not only when we look at the composition of soldiers, but when we look at the composition of the generals, and this was ten years later. So why are you falsifying facts? Why are you manipulating facts in this way? You know that the JNA then had members in proportion to the ethnic -- general ethnic make-up, as far as soldiers go and also as far as generals go. There were even more from other republics than there were from Serbia. This was a Yugoslav army. You yourself said it was an integrating factor. So it doesn't make sense when you say that it was Serbia who took the JNA under its command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Another speech. Another speech. It's said that you're wrong about the ethnic make-up, Mr. Mesic. It says you're wrong about it in 1999 and 2000, but we're not dealing with those years. But dealing with the years which we are talking about, which would be 1991, can you give any evidence about the ethnic make-up, or are you relying on the behaviour of the army, your evidence about it becoming more Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the Croats in the JNA left it when it became evident that the JNA was waging an aggressive war against the Republic of Croatia. Most of the Slovenians in the JNA left it when it became completely evident that the army was waging an aggressive war against Slovenia. The same happened in the case of other republics. Whether a few individuals remained is of less importance. Some individuals did remain. I assert that too. But the army was implementing a policy that General Kadijevic admits was aimed at setting up a Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag boundary. This is what General Kadijevic himself said, regardless of who his father and mother were. I'm not interested in that. But he was in the service of the greater Serbian policy and the aggression against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume that General Kadijevic can testify about that and not you, Mr. Mesic. In its public announcement of the 1st of October, its communique, did your Presidency express concern because the federal organs and the assembly were no longer functioning, the Presidency was undergoing a crisis, and the president wanted to have extended sessions to be attended by representatives of the republic and federal governments and so on? Do you remember this? This is on page 8, paragraph 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I was in Belgrade at the time, but it's quite clear that the federal institutions were not in fact functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the session of the 3rd of October, the Presidency stated that Yugoslavia was facing an imminent threat of war and that this was not a session of a Rump Presidency but a session attended by six members of the Presidency? Is it not true that this was functioning in danger of imminent threat of war and that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would Mr. Milosevic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. Yugoslavia was not facing an imminent threat of war. Yugoslavia was threatened by Serbian aggression against parts of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, apart from these political qualifications which are quite inadequate, you have no arguments to put forward. You are speaking of a war against Yugoslavia, an illegal and unconstitutional secession, it's expulsion of units of the Yugoslav army from the territory of Croatia. Please, your fabrication about what General Kadijevic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're not here to listen to more speeches. We're almost finished today. It may be of assistance to know how long do you think you might require in re-examination, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It could be 20 minutes I thought would have been more than possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There will be that available. We'll have to decide how the time goes is to be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are important issues raised with this witness and it's only right that a proper record should be left in the evidence about what the true position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, would you be available for longer than one hour tomorrow morning? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to be in Zagreb by 12.00 noon. I need at least an hour to get there, or an hour and a half, to get to Zagreb. Maybe an hour and a half. I could be here for an hour and a half, from 9.00 to 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be helpful. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll give the accused another half hour had, Mr. Tapuskovic half an hour, Prosecution 20 minutes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You've got another five minutes. Do you want to ask some more questions, Mr. Milosevic, this afternoon, or are you finished for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Mesic: Were your claim correct, what sort of obligation would the army have to obey me had I ordered the army, the then JNA, to do something? Why would they have had to obey me? How could I have issued them with orders?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally they were under no obligation. That's precisely the point. You issued orders to that army, and when I asked General Kadijevic why he was obeying only you, he said: Everybody else in Serbia is even worse. You should discuss this with General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you asked him why he was communicating with me at all, not why he was obeying me. Because, as you know, that is untrue.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Kadijevic, as the Secretary of National Defence, never, throughout my term of office in Belgrade, came to see me. Just recall how many times you talked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Less than you, I assume as his supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're making me laugh again. This is no place for us to laugh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 17 of your statement, you say that the Rump Presidency implemented a putsch, a coup d'etat. Was this a Rump Presidency because you obstructed its functioning and those who followed you in your obstruction, or was it a Rump Presidency because those who continued to attend the sessions were continuing to fulfil their obligations? Was it a Rump Presidency because you left it or because they remained at their posts performing their duty? Is there any logic in this, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: STJEPAN MESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rump Presidency could not be established by any legal and legitimate means, by any extensive interpretations of the constitution. This was an illegal group of people which introduced a state of emergency, at the suggestion of Slobodan Milosevic, because he was the only one who had any influence over those people and over that Rump Presidency. And let me give you a piece of information. My advisor remained in Belgrade. The room, the premises where the Presidency and later the Rump Presidency had its sessions had a connecting door leading to my former cabinet. My advisor listened to what they were talking about. He came to Croatia by way of Hungary and reported to me, so that I knew what the Rump Presidency was discussing. Slobodan Milosevic asked that Vukovar be left alone and that the army go to Zagreb. And General Kadijevic said that this was impossible because the Croats had gained in military strength to such an extent that they would attack his flanks and he would not be able to reach Zagreb. So the opinion prevailed in the end that Vukovar had to be destroyed. This is my interpretation now, but it was the accused who asked that Zagreb be attacked. The witness to this is my advisor who told me this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's follow this. When were you told that there had been this discussion about Vukovar, Mr. Mesic? What sort of date are we dealing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the time when I was not going to Belgrade, when there were frequent army attacks from Novi Sad and Belgrade against Vukovar, and my advisor was still in Belgrade. He was in Belgrade until Vukovar fell. And he used to come to see me by way of Hungary, via Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, do you know that the presidents of the republics at the session of the Presidency, that they arrived only rarely and by invitation, and that except on those rare occasions when all the other presidents of the republics were present, I never took part in any sessions of the Presidency? How can you put forward such fabrications, such falsehoods? You should know that. And you say this was put to you by your advisor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's suggested, Mr. Mesic, that this is not true. Perhaps you could answer that and then we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I have to say that the accused is now speculating. These are not sessions of the Presidency of the SFRY, because I know very well how any session chaired by me was convocated [As interpreted]. I'm speaking about sessions of the Rump Presidency. Who they invited and how, I don't know. I only know what my advisor told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to adjourn now. It's 2.00. Tomorrow morning -- you can go on tomorrow morning about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we adjourn and before too late, I'd like to suggest the registrar to exhibit Mr. Mesic's transcript the in Dokmanovic, which we didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe it was marked Exhibit 329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those are exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will look into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the position is that part of the transcript was marked on its side as exhibited pursuant to the 92 bis package and the other part wasn't. So there might be grounds for simply taking the whole Dokmanovic transcript and exhibiting it as His Honour Judge Kwon proposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. First of all, we'll deal with the exhibit number. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution's Exhibit 331.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked that the other transcript, which contains a more extensive testimony by Mr. Mesic, also be tendered into evidence. I will not say what the case is, because he was a protected witness in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't seen that. Is there any objection to that being done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I think about that over night. One of my problems is is that in two cases the page references of the accused don't match the transcript I have and I haven't been able to find the references he made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that overnight. Meanwhile, I would remind everybody that we are sitting tomorrow from 9.00 in the morning until half past 4.00, 4.00 to half past tomorrow, 4.00 or half past tomorrow. Mr. Mesic, would you be back, please, for the first session tomorrow. Thank you. 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of October 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25
